1	# 14 — Session Recap: Hardware Bring-Up + 3D Spin (2026-07-22)
2	
3	> Catch-up doc for a fresh Claude session (e.g. on another machine). Read this
4	> first, then dig into the referenced files as needed.
5	
6	## Who/what
7	
8	Nikolas is building this middleware to add multi-sport ball detection,
9	tracking, and spin to an AccuGolf Hawkeye 2-camera rig, streaming results to
10	Unity games over UDP. This session happened on-site at the actual hardware,
11	which resolved most of the previously-unknown physical setup, and then built
12	out real spin measurement.
13	
14	**Games in scope:** soccer, hockey, baseball, football (field-goal kicks
15	only, not thrown spirals), possibly lacrosse. **Golf is explicitly
16	out of scope** — the AccuGolf Hawkeye already handles it natively; this
17	middleware is for everything else.
18	
19	## Confirmed hardware facts (do not re-ask)
20	
21	- **Spinnaker SDK**: `C:\Program Files\Teledyne\Spinnaker\bin64\vs2015\`, SDK 4.2.0.83. Single managed assembly `SpinnakerNET_v140.dll` (not two DLLs like older SDKs) — wired into [SportSimulator.csproj](../SportSimulator.csproj).
22	- **Camera model**: Blackfly S BFS-PGE-04S2M, **monochrome** (Mono8 native, no color/Bayer data available — matters if any sport ever wants color-based detection).
23	- **Resolution**: 720×540, **fixed/locked — no ROI windowing available**. This closes off "higher fps via a smaller ROI" as a path to real spin for fast-spinning sports (see Spin section below).
24	- **Frame rate**: confirmed 199.76fps at default (full-frame) settings.
25	- **Stereo baseline**: 19.5in center-to-center = 0.4953m.
26	- **Mounting geometry**: sensor 114in above floor, 33in horizontally forward of the tee/ball spot → tilt ≈16.15° off nadir (≈73.85° off horizontal). **No yaw** (confirmed via SpinView sightline check against the real shot line), no lateral offset.
27	- **Camera roles**: left = serial 24182871, right = serial 24193779. Spinnaker's raw enumeration order does NOT reliably match this — [CameraManager.cs](../Vision/CameraManager.cs) assigns `CameraIndex` by serial number (`SerialToCameraIndex` map) rather than trusting enumeration order. **Update that map if a camera is ever swapped.**
28	- **Trigger config**: SpinView reported `TriggerSource=Software`, ambiguous whether `TriggerMode` was On (which would silently starve the app of frames — nothing calls a software trigger). Fixed defensively: `CameraManager` now forces `TriggerMode=Off` explicitly regardless of the camera's persisted state.
29	
30	## Real bugs found + fixed this session
31	
32	- `net48` had **never actually compiled** before this session — multiple real API mismatches against the installed SDK (logging handler signature, `GetTLStreamNodeMap()` not `GetStreamNodeMap()`, `.ManagedData` not `.GetData()`), plus .NET Framework doesn't have `MathF`/`Math.Clamp` (added [Compat/NetFrameworkCompat.cs](../Compat/NetFrameworkCompat.cs) polyfill), plus a `record` type needing `IsExternalInit` (swapped for a tuple in [StereoCalibrator.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrator.cs)).
33	- **Camera left/right was backwards** — see camera roles above. Would have silently degraded all real detections to low-confidence monocular tracking.
34	- `StereoRectifier` was built at startup but **never actually applied to frames** — triangulation was running on unrectified coordinates. Fixed in [SimulatorEngine.cs](../App/SimulatorEngine.cs) (`RectifyFrame`), which is also a hard prerequisite for the 3D spin work (needs epipolar-rectified rows for stereo point matching).
35	- `fy = fx * (cy/cx)` in [StereoCalibrationData.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrationData.cs) was mathematically wrong for a square-pixel sensor (fy should just equal fx, independent of aspect ratio) — fixed, regression test added.
36	- `net48`'s `UdpClient` has no cancellable `ReceiveAsync(CancellationToken)` — [UdpTransport.cs](../Transport/UdpTransport.cs) now uses the standard close-the-socket cancellation pattern (works on both targets).
37	- `FindStereoMatch`'s original fixed 60px disparity search window was far too small for this rig's real geometry (~289px expected disparity at the ball spot, ranging ~170–870px across a shot's depth). Now searches around an *expected* disparity derived from the ball's own just-triangulated position each frame.
38	- Normalized correlation is degenerate (spurious high-confidence match) on a textureless patch — added a variance guard in [FeaturePointTracker.cs](../Vision/FeaturePointTracker.cs).
39	
40	## Spin measurement — two tiers, know the difference
41	
42	**Why two systems exist:** a single camera watching from nearly overhead can only see rotation about its own viewing axis. Backspin/topspin and a tumbling field-goal kick both rotate about a *horizontal* axis lying in the image plane — invisible to simple 2D correlation from this rig's mounting angle. Sidespin/curl (vertical axis) is the one case simple 2D correlation handles well here.
43	
44	1. **[SpinEstimator.cs](../Vision/SpinEstimator.cs)** — single-camera 2D rotation correlation. Magnitude only, no axis. Reliable only where spin rate stays under ~90°/frame at 200fps (soccer's ~300–600rpm; NOT golf/baseball/tennis, which alias badly — and golf/tennis are out of scope anyway).
45	2. **[RotationFitter.cs](../Tracking/RotationFitter.cs) + [FeaturePointTracker.cs](../Vision/FeaturePointTracker.cs) + [Spin3DEstimator.cs](../Vision/Spin3DEstimator.cs)** — full 3D spin (magnitude AND axis), built this session. Natural-texture tracking (GFTT corners + optical flow + rectified stereo matching + Kabsch rigid-rotation fit), not marked/painted balls — chosen to avoid a practice-ball workflow change. Wired into `SimulatorEngine`; populates `BallData.SpinAxisX/Y/Z` for the first time. Takes priority over the 2D estimate when it produces a valid fit.
46	
47	**Both are covered by unit tests against synthetic data (149 tests total, all passing) — this proves the math and wiring are correct. It does NOT prove real ball surfaces have enough natural texture contrast at 720×540 under real lighting for GFTT to track reliably. That's the biggest open unknown, only checkable against real footage.**
48	
49	Ball choice matters: cameras are monochrome, so only grayscale contrast counts, not color. A classic black/white pentagon ball is the safer bet — a modern colorful ball can look flat/featureless in grayscale even if it looks richly patterned to the eye.
50	
51	**Live validation added:** `SimulatorEngine` now prints `[Spin3D] rpm=... axis=(x,y,z) points=N` every time the 3D fit succeeds (unthrottled — whether this line appears at all is itself diagnostic), and a throttled `[Ball] pos=... speed=... tier=... spin=...` trajectory line (~10Hz) during tracking. To sanity-check axis output against real shots: a pure backspin shot should show `axis.X` dominant; a pure sidespin/curl shot should show `axis.Z` dominant with a smaller `axis.Y` (~±0.28, from the known 16.15° tilt) — not noise, expected geometry. `AxisUnit` is camera-relative, not yet rotated into labeled backspin/sidespin/spiral terms.
52	
53	## Sport-specific spin decisions
54	
55	- **Soccer**: real spin wanted and achievable (2D or 3D).
56	- **Football**: field-goal kicks only (no thrown spirals in scope) → backspin/tumble case, needs the 3D method.
57	- **Baseball**: spin/curve explicitly ignored — assume straight flight.
58	- **Hockey**: no spin needed (`OutputSpin = false` already in its profile) — pucks don't backspin meaningfully.
59	- **Lacrosse**: no solid spin-rate reference data; likely fine at 200fps if wanted, but low confidence — probably treat like baseball (ignore) unless proven otherwise.
60	- **Tennis**: dropped from scope entirely (that game won't be made).
61	
62	## Still open / not done
63	
64	1. **Real checkerboard calibration hasn't been run.** Everything currently runs on computed-from-measurements fallback defaults (baseline, resolution confirmed exactly; focal length only approximated from a floor-FOV measurement). No runnable calibration CLI exists yet — just the `StereoCalibrator` class. Offered to build a small harness; not done.
65	2. **Exposure tuning** — [CameraManager.cs](../Vision/CameraManager.cs)'s per-sport exposure map is still placeholder values; needs live SpinView tuning against real lighting.
66	3. **`KalmanCoastFrames`** ([SportProfileRegistry.cs](../Profiles/SportProfileRegistry.cs)) were tuned assuming 120fps; real fps is ~200, so the same frame counts now mean shorter real-world coast windows than originally intended. Not yet recomputed — open decision, not yet raised with Nikolas again since the calibration/spin work took priority.
67	4. **Unity-side readiness is unknown** — this repo only handles camera → detection → UDP send (`BallData`/`ProfileSelectCommand`, wire format in [PacketSerializer.cs](../Transport/PacketSerializer.cs), default ports 7100 send / 7101 listen). Whether the Unity soccer game already has a receiver for this is outside this repo and hasn't been confirmed.
68	5. **Must run the net48 build for real cameras** — [Program.cs](../App/Program.cs) picks real Spinnaker vs `MockCameraManager` based on compiled target framework, not a runtime flag. `dotnet run` can easily end up building `net10.0-windows` (mock/synthetic data) instead. Use `dotnet build -f net48` then run the `.exe` directly from `bin\...\net48\`, or run via Visual Studio targeting net48.
69	
70	## Related
71	
72	- [README (index)](README.md) · [00 Project Vision](00-project-vision.md)
73	- [11 Unity Integration](11-unity-integration.md) — the wire-protocol design this session actually implemented
74	- [12 Implementation Roadmap](12-implementation-roadmap.md)

## Sport-specific spin decisions

- **Soccer**: real spin wanted and achievable (2D or 3D).
- **Football**: field-goal kicks only (no thrown spirals in scope) → backspin/tumble case, needs the 3D method.
- **Baseball**: spin/curve explicitly ignored — assume straight flight.
- **Hockey**: no spin needed (`OutputSpin = false` already in its profile) — pucks don't backspin meaningfully.
- **Lacrosse**: no solid spin-rate reference data; likely fine at 200fps if wanted, but low confidence — probably treat like baseball (ignore) unless proven otherwise.
- **Tennis**: dropped from scope entirely (that game won't be made).

## Still open / not done

1. **Real checkerboard calibration hasn't been run.** Everything currently runs on computed-from-measurements fallback defaults (baseline, resolution confirmed exactly; focal length only approximated from a floor-FOV measurement). No runnable calibration CLI exists yet — just the `StereoCalibrator` class. Offered to build a small harness; not done.
2. **Exposure tuning** — [CameraManager.cs](../Vision/CameraManager.cs)'s per-sport exposure map is still placeholder values; needs live SpinView tuning against real lighting.
3. **`KalmanCoastFrames`** ([SportProfileRegistry.cs](../Profiles/SportProfileRegistry.cs)) were tuned assuming 120fps; real fps is ~200, so the same frame counts now mean shorter real-world coast windows than originally intended. Not yet recomputed — open decision, not yet raised with Nikolas again since the calibration/spin work took priority.
4. **Unity-side readiness is unknown** — this repo only handles camera → detection → UDP send (`BallData`/`ProfileSelectCommand`, wire format in [PacketSerializer.cs](../Transport/PacketSerializer.cs), default ports 7100 send / 7101 listen). Whether the Unity soccer game already has a receiver for this is outside this repo and hasn't been confirmed.
5. **Must run the net48 build for real cameras** — [Program.cs](../App/Program.cs) picks real Spinnaker vs `MockCameraManager` based on compiled target framework, not a runtime flag. `dotnet run` can easily end up building `net10.0-windows` (mock/synthetic data) instead. Use `dotnet build -f net48` then run the `.exe` directly from `bin\...\net48\`, or run via Visual Studio targeting net48.

## Related

- [README (index)](README.md) · [00 Project Vision](00-project-vision.md)
- [11 Unity Integration](11-unity-integration.md) — the wire-protocol design this session actually implemented
- [12 Implementation Roadmap](12-implementation-roadmap.md)

2	
3	> Spinnaker is C/C++/C#/.NET. Unity is C#. Three reasonable shapes for the bridge.
4	
5	> ⚠️ This note is **design speculation** — the user hasn't picked an approach yet. Confirm before coding.
6	
7	## Option A — Native middleware process + UDP/WebSocket
8	
9	**Architecture:**
10	```
11	[ C++ or C# middleware ] ──UDP/JSON──▶ [ Unity game ]
12	       Spinnaker SDK                       UDP listener
13	       OpenCV
14	```
15	
16	**Pros**
17	- Clean separation: middleware can be restarted without restarting Unity.
18	- Middleware can be heavy (OpenCV, CUDA, ML) without bloating the Unity build.
19	- Multiple Unity instances (or other clients) can subscribe.
20	
21	**Cons**
22	- Serialization overhead per shot (small — single JSON / protobuf per shot).
23	- IPC plumbing.
24	
25	**When**: Default choice. Pick this unless there's a specific reason.
26	
27	## Option B — Spinnaker C# SDK directly in Unity
28	
29	**Architecture:**
30	```
31	[ Unity game (C#) ]
32	   ├─ Spinnaker .NET binding (Managed SDK)
33	   ├─ OpenCV via OpenCVSharp / EmguCV
34	   └─ Game logic
35	```
36	
37	**Pros**
38	- No IPC, no serialization, no two processes to manage.
39	- Easier to ship to customers (single installer).
40	
41	**Cons**
42	- Spinnaker uses callbacks on its own threads — Unity main loop is single-threaded. Must marshal results back via `UnitySynchronizationContext` or a queue read on `Update()`.
43	- Heavy CV work in the same process can stall the renderer.
44	- Spinnaker is `net48` / WinForms-flavored — verify it works with Unity's runtime (Mono / IL2CPP).
45	
46	**When**: Single-customer simulator boxes where simplicity wins.
47	
48	## Option C — Native DLL + Unity P/Invoke
49	
50	**Architecture:**
51	```
52	[ Unity (C#) ] ─P/Invoke─▶ [ native middleware.dll (C++) ]
53	                              Spinnaker SDK, OpenCV
54	```
55	
56	**Pros**
57	- Performance-first. Heavy CV runs in native code.
58	- Spinnaker is happiest in C++.
59	
60	**Cons**
61	- Marshalling pinned image buffers across the managed/native boundary is delicate.
62	- Crashes in native code take down Unity.
63	
64	**When**: Performance is critical, team has native-dev experience.
65	
66	## Recommended data payload (shot record)
67	
68	After each detected shot, emit something like:
69	
70	```json
71	{
72	  "shotId": "2026-05-25T22:10:33Z-001",
73	  "timestampNs": 18293749234,
74	  "ball": {
75	    "ballSpeed_mps": 71.2,
76	    "launchAngle_deg": 11.4,
77	    "azimuth_deg": -0.8,
78	    "totalSpin_rpm": 2730,
79	    "backSpin_rpm": 2680,
80	    "sideSpin_rpm": -540
81	  },
82	  "club": {
83	    "clubSpeed_mps": 49.6,
84	    "attackAngle_deg": -2.1,
85	    "clubPath_deg": 0.8,
86	    "faceAngle_deg": 0.4,
87	    "faceToPath_deg": -0.4,
88	    "impactPosX_mm": 2.3,
89	    "impactPosY_mm": -1.1
90	  },
91	  "quality": {
92	    "ballConfidence": 0.94,
93	    "clubConfidence": 0.81,
94	    "framesUsed": 6
95	  }
96	}
97	```
98	
99	This roughly matches the data fields commercial launch monitors (TrackMan, GCQuad, Foresight) expose. Unity can render flight from `ballSpeed`, `launchAngle`, `azimuth`, and the three spins.
100	
101	## Frame rate vs shot rate
102	
103	The camera streams hundreds of fps continuously, but a shot **event** happens once every ~5 seconds. The middleware should:
104	
105	1. **Free-run** the camera in a low-cost "armed" state (or trigger-only mode).
106	2. **On trigger** (break-beam / sound), capture a burst of N frames at full speed (see [04 Trigger](04-hardware-triggering.md), burst mode).
107	3. **Process** the burst into a shot record.
108	4. **Emit** one message to Unity.
109	
110	Unity doesn't need raw frames — it needs the shot result.
111

113

# 11 — Unity Integration

> Spinnaker is C/C++/C#/.NET. Unity is C#. Three reasonable shapes for the bridge.

> ⚠️ This note is **design speculation** — the user hasn't picked an approach yet. Confirm before coding.

## Option A — Native middleware process + UDP/WebSocket

**Architecture:**
```
[ C++ or C# middleware ] ──UDP/JSON──▶ [ Unity game ]
       Spinnaker SDK                       UDP listener
       OpenCV
```

**Pros**
- Clean separation: middleware can be restarted without restarting Unity.
- Middleware can be heavy (OpenCV, CUDA, ML) without bloating the Unity build.
- Multiple Unity instances (or other clients) can subscribe.

**Cons**
- Serialization overhead per shot (small — single JSON / protobuf per shot).
- IPC plumbing.

**When**: Default choice. Pick this unless there's a specific reason.

## Option B — Spinnaker C# SDK directly in Unity

**Architecture:**
```
[ Unity game (C#) ]
   ├─ Spinnaker .NET binding (Managed SDK)
   ├─ OpenCV via OpenCVSharp / EmguCV
   └─ Game logic
```

**Pros**
- No IPC, no serialization, no two processes to manage.
- Easier to ship to customers (single installer).

**Cons**
- Spinnaker uses callbacks on its own threads — Unity main loop is single-threaded. Must marshal results back via `UnitySynchronizationContext` or a queue read on `Update()`.
- Heavy CV work in the same process can stall the renderer.
- Spinnaker is `net48` / WinForms-flavored — verify it works with Unity's runtime (Mono / IL2CPP).

**When**: Single-customer simulator boxes where simplicity wins.

## Option C — Native DLL + Unity P/Invoke

**Architecture:**
```
[ Unity (C#) ] ─P/Invoke─▶ [ native middleware.dll (C++) ]
                              Spinnaker SDK, OpenCV
```

**Pros**
- Performance-first. Heavy CV runs in native code.
- Spinnaker is happiest in C++.

**Cons**
- Marshalling pinned image buffers across the managed/native boundary is delicate.
- Crashes in native code take down Unity.

**When**: Performance is critical, team has native-dev experience.

## Recommended data payload (shot record)

After each detected shot, emit something like:

```json
{
  "shotId": "2026-05-25T22:10:33Z-001",
  "timestampNs": 18293749234,
  "ball": {
    "ballSpeed_mps": 71.2,
    "launchAngle_deg": 11.4,
    "azimuth_deg": -0.8,
    "totalSpin_rpm": 2730,
    "backSpin_rpm": 2680,
    "sideSpin_rpm": -540
  },
  "club": {
    "clubSpeed_mps": 49.6,
    "attackAngle_deg": -2.1,
    "clubPath_deg": 0.8,
    "faceAngle_deg": 0.4,
    "faceToPath_deg": -0.4,
    "impactPosX_mm": 2.3,
    "impactPosY_mm": -1.1
  },
  "quality": {
    "ballConfidence": 0.94,
    "clubConfidence": 0.81,
    "framesUsed": 6
  }
}
```

This roughly matches the data fields commercial launch monitors (TrackMan, GCQuad, Foresight) expose. Unity can render flight from `ballSpeed`, `launchAngle`, `azimuth`, and the three spins.

## Frame rate vs shot rate

The camera streams hundreds of fps continuously, but a shot **event** happens once every ~5 seconds. The middleware should:

1. **Free-run** the camera in a low-cost "armed" state (or trigger-only mode).
2. **On trigger** (break-beam / sound), capture a burst of N frames at full speed (see [04 Trigger](04-hardware-triggering.md), burst mode).
3. **Process** the burst into a shot record.
4. **Emit** one message to Unity.

Unity doesn't need raw frames — it needs the shot result.

## Optional: live preview to Unity

For technician calibration / aim setup, you might want a low-rate live frame stream too. Encode as JPEG and stream over WebSocket at ~30 fps. Don't pump raw frames through IPC — encoding pays for itself many times over.

# 14 — Session Recap: Hardware Bring-Up + 3D Spin (2026-07-22)

> Catch-up doc for a fresh Claude session (e.g. on another machine). Read this
> first, then dig into the referenced files as needed.

## Who/what

Nikolas is building this middleware to add multi-sport ball detection,
tracking, and spin to an AccuGolf Hawkeye 2-camera rig, streaming results to
Unity games over UDP. This session happened on-site at the actual hardware,
which resolved most of the previously-unknown physical setup, and then built
out real spin measurement.

**Games in scope:** soccer, hockey, baseball, football (field-goal kicks
only, not thrown spirals), possibly lacrosse. **Golf is explicitly
out of scope** — the AccuGolf Hawkeye already handles it natively; this
middleware is for everything else.

## Confirmed hardware facts (do not re-ask)

- **Spinnaker SDK**: `C:\Program Files\Teledyne\Spinnaker\bin64\vs2015\`, SDK 4.2.0.83. Single managed assembly `SpinnakerNET_v140.dll` (not two DLLs like older SDKs) — wired into [SportSimulator.csproj](../SportSimulator.csproj).
- **Camera model**: Blackfly S BFS-PGE-04S2M, **monochrome** (Mono8 native, no color/Bayer data available — matters if any sport ever wants color-based detection).
- **Resolution**: 720×540, **fixed/locked — no ROI windowing available**. This closes off "higher fps via a smaller ROI" as a path to real spin for fast-spinning sports (see Spin section below).
- **Frame rate**: confirmed 199.76fps at default (full-frame) settings.
- **Stereo baseline**: 19.5in center-to-center = 0.4953m.
- **Mounting geometry**: sensor 114in above floor, 33in horizontally forward of the tee/ball spot → tilt ≈16.15° off nadir (≈73.85° off horizontal). **No yaw** (confirmed via SpinView sightline check against the real shot line), no lateral offset.
- **Camera roles**: left = serial 24182871, right = serial 24193779. Spinnaker's raw enumeration order does NOT reliably match this — [CameraManager.cs](../Vision/CameraManager.cs) assigns `CameraIndex` by serial number (`SerialToCameraIndex` map) rather than trusting enumeration order. **Update that map if a camera is ever swapped.**
- **Trigger config**: SpinView reported `TriggerSource=Software`, ambiguous whether `TriggerMode` was On (which would silently starve the app of frames — nothing calls a software trigger). Fixed defensively: `CameraManager` now forces `TriggerMode=Off` explicitly regardless of the camera's persisted state.

## Real bugs found + fixed this session

- `net48` had **never actually compiled** before this session — multiple real API mismatches against the installed SDK (logging handler signature, `GetTLStreamNodeMap()` not `GetStreamNodeMap()`, `.ManagedData` not `.GetData()`), plus .NET Framework doesn't have `MathF`/`Math.Clamp` (added [Compat/NetFrameworkCompat.cs](../Compat/NetFrameworkCompat.cs) polyfill), plus a `record` type needing `IsExternalInit` (swapped for a tuple in [StereoCalibrator.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrator.cs)).
- **Camera left/right was backwards** — see camera roles above. Would have silently degraded all real detections to low-confidence monocular tracking.
- `StereoRectifier` was built at startup but **never actually applied to frames** — triangulation was running on unrectified coordinates. Fixed in [SimulatorEngine.cs](../App/SimulatorEngine.cs) (`RectifyFrame`), which is also a hard prerequisite for the 3D spin work (needs epipolar-rectified rows for stereo point matching).
- `fy = fx * (cy/cx)` in [StereoCalibrationData.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrationData.cs) was mathematically wrong for a square-pixel sensor (fy should just equal fx, independent of aspect ratio) — fixed, regression test added.
- `net48`'s `UdpClient` has no cancellable `ReceiveAsync(CancellationToken)` — [UdpTransport.cs](../Transport/UdpTransport.cs) now uses the standard close-the-socket cancellation pattern (works on both targets).
- `FindStereoMatch`'s original fixed 60px disparity search window was far too small for this rig's real geometry (~289px expected disparity at the ball spot, ranging ~170–870px across a shot's depth). Now searches around an *expected* disparity derived from the ball's own just-triangulated position each frame.
- Normalized correlation is degenerate (spurious high-confidence match) on a textureless patch — added a variance guard in [FeaturePointTracker.cs](../Vision/FeaturePointTracker.cs).

## Spin measurement — two tiers, know the difference

**Why two systems exist:** a single camera watching from nearly overhead can only see rotation about its own viewing axis. Backspin/topspin and a tumbling field-goal kick both rotate about a *horizontal* axis lying in the image plane — invisible to simple 2D correlation from this rig's mounting angle. Sidespin/curl (vertical axis) is the one case simple 2D correlation handles well here.

1. **[SpinEstimator.cs](../Vision/SpinEstimator.cs)** — single-camera 2D rotation correlation. Magnitude only, no axis. Reliable only where spin rate stays under ~90°/frame at 200fps (soccer's ~300–600rpm; NOT golf/baseball/tennis, which alias badly — and golf/tennis are out of scope anyway).
2. **[RotationFitter.cs](../Tracking/RotationFitter.cs) + [FeaturePointTracker.cs](../Vision/FeaturePointTracker.cs) + [Spin3DEstimator.cs](../Vision/Spin3DEstimator.cs)** — full 3D spin (magnitude AND axis), built this session. Natural-texture tracking (GFTT corners + optical flow + rectified stereo matching + Kabsch rigid-rotation fit), not marked/painted balls — chosen to avoid a practice-ball workflow change. Wired into `SimulatorEngine`; populates `BallData.SpinAxisX/Y/Z` for the first time. Takes priority over the 2D estimate when it produces a valid fit.

**Both are covered by unit tests against synthetic data (149 tests total, all passing) — this proves the math and wiring are correct. It does NOT prove real ball surfaces have enough natural texture contrast at 720×540 under real lighting for GFTT to track reliably. That's the biggest open unknown, only checkable against real footage.**

Ball choice matters: cameras are monochrome, so only grayscale contrast counts, not color. A classic black/white pentagon ball is the safer bet — a modern colorful ball can look flat/featureless in grayscale even if it looks richly patterned to the eye.

**Live validation added:** `SimulatorEngine` now prints `[Spin3D] rpm=... axis=(x,y,z) points=N` every time the 3D fit succeeds (unthrottled — whether this line appears at all is itself diagnostic), and a throttled `[Ball] pos=... speed=... tier=... spin=...` trajectory line (~10Hz) during tracking. To sanity-check axis output against real shots: a pure backspin shot should show `axis.X` dominant; a pure sidespin/curl shot should show `axis.Z` dominant with a smaller `axis.Y` (~±0.28, from the known 16.15° tilt) — not noise, expected geometry. `AxisUnit` is camera-relative, not yet rotated into labeled backspin/sidespin/spiral terms.

## Sport-specific spin decisions

- **Soccer**: real spin wanted and achievable (2D or 3D).
- **Football**: field-goal kicks only (no thrown spirals in scope) → backspin/tumble case, needs the 3D method.
- **Baseball**: spin/curve explicitly ignored — assume straight flight.
- **Hockey**: no spin needed (`OutputSpin = false` already in its profile) — pucks don't backspin meaningfully.
- **Lacrosse**: no solid spin-rate reference data; likely fine at 200fps if wanted, but low confidence — probably treat like baseball (ignore) unless proven otherwise.
- **Tennis**: dropped from scope entirely (that game won't be made).

1. **Real checkerboard calibration hasn't been run.** Everything currently runs on computed-from-measurements fallback defaults (baseline, resolution confirmed exactly; focal length only approximated from a floor-FOV measurement). No runnable calibration CLI exists yet — just the `StereoCalibrator` class. Offered to build a small harness; not done.

3. **`KalmanCoastFrames`** ([SportProfileRegistry.cs](../Profiles/SportProfileRegistry.cs)) were tuned assuming 120fps; real fps is ~200, so the same frame counts now mean shorter real-world coast windows than originally intended. I'm thinking through the UDP connection semantics here. Since UDP is connectionless, the middleware can start sending packets to 127.0.0.1:7100 without any actual connection being established—those early packets just get dropped if Unity hasn't bound to that port yet, with no errors or queuing involved.

The critical issue is that MockCameraManager generates frames for exactly 2 seconds (based on fps*2 frameCount), then stops completely—it's a one-time synthetic shot, not a repeating loop. So if the middleware starts first and Unity isn't listening yet, the entire 2-second trajectory gets missed, and since the frame generation never restarts, nothing else will ever be sent. That's actually a significant problem for the startup order. So the ProfileSelectSender does retry every couple seconds for about 10 seconds, which handles most startup timing issues, but the BallData listener in Unity has no such mechanism—the middleware just streams once per frame and if nobody's listening, that data's lost. Since MockCameraManager only generates one 2-second synthetic flight right after engine startup, the window is extremely tight, making the startup order critical: launch Unity first so its listener is already bound to port 7100 before the middleware even starts firing data.

Let me verify the actual startup sequence in the Start() method to see how much buffer time exists between when the UDP transport initializes and when the mock camera begins generating frames.

So StartCapture() immediately kicks off frame generation through a background task with roughly 5ms intervals between frames at 200fps, which means detection starts almost instantly. The first frame per camera gets used as a background reference for motion detection, so actual ball detection begins from the second frame onward — and since the mock blob only appears once the ball moves into the frame, there's minimal delay before BallData starts flowing over UDP.

The key point: UDP is connectionless, so there's no handshake or connection failure. But that's exactly the problem — packets sent while nothing's listening on that port are silently dropped by the OS. The middleware doesn't queue, retry, or even know they were lost, so if Unity isn't already listening when the middleware starts sending, those early frames are just gone.

The practical implication is that the mock camera fires a one-time 2-second shot right when the middleware starts, so if Unity isn't in Play mode listening on port 7100 yet, you'll miss that entire test shot and have to restart the middleware to see it again. The safe approach is to start Unity first to bind the port, then start the middleware. Going the other direction is less critical since Unity's ProfileSelectSender retries every 2 seconds for about 10 seconds, giving the middleware time to come up and start listening on 7101.

With real hardware, this timing concern mostly disappears because the detection loop runs continuously and indefinitely rather than firing once, so the middleware will just keep streaming tracked data whenever a ball is present—starting Unity late just means missing some earlier frames, not missing everything. But for this mock test specifically, the startup order really does matter.

I should verify that the UDP receiver binds the port when the MonoBehaviour starts—yes, it does, and there's no retry logic beyond that initial bind. content.text:
Start Unity first, then the middleware — order matters here, and not for the reason you might expect.

UDP is connectionless — there's no handshake to "establish." A socket just binds to a port and either something is listening or it isn't. If the middleware sends a packet to port 7100 and nothing's bound there yet, the packet is silently dropped — no error on the sender side, no queuing, no retry. The middleware has zero awareness of whether Unity is listening.

That alone wouldn't be a big deal for continuous real-hardware use (it just streams live tracked data forever, so late-joining Unity only misses whatever happened before it connected). But for your **mock test specifically**, it's a bigger problem: `MockCameraManager.GenerateFrames` fires exactly **one** synthetic 2-second shot the moment `StartCapture()` runs, then stops generating frames entirely — it doesn't loop. That happens within milliseconds of you running `dotnet run`. If Unity's `UdpReceiverNew` isn't already bound to port 7100 at that point, you miss the entire shot and have to restart the middleware process to get another one.

So:

Since the throttled logging only triggers after 20 successful sends, even the first detection should've produced a log line within a couple seconds given the mock generates ~400 frames over 2 seconds at ~200fps. This points to detection failing 100% of the time throughout the flight—Found consistently returns false—which means either the area filter is rejecting every contour, frames aren't making it into the queue properly, RectifyFrame is silently failing, or something else is blocking the pipeline before it reaches the Send call. I'm starting to suspect the real culprit might be a calibration or rectification bug.

The issue could be that RectifyFrame itself is broken because InitUndistortRectifyMap was called with an all-zero P0 matrix (since P0 was never populated by an actual StereoRectify call). Feeding a degenerate zero projection matrix into that function would generate garbage remap tables full of NaN or out-of-bounds values, and then applying those corrupted maps during the remap operation would produce an all-black or garbage rectified image—meaning by the time BallDetector runs on it, there's no visible ball blob left to detect.

This theory actually explains the consistent detection failure much better than the shared-background hypothesis, and it points directly back to the root bug: StereoRectifier.Build() never actually calls StereoRectify to compute real R0/R1/P0/P1/Q values—it just uses whatever's already in the calibration object (all zeros from CreateDefaults), feeding those degenerate matrices downstream.

When InitUndistortRectifyMap gets a P matrix that's all zeros instead of valid focal lengths, it can't compute proper remap tables—it likely produces degenerate mappings with NaN or zero coordinates for every pixel, causing Remap to sample from invalid locations and output mostly black or garbage frames instead of properly rectified images.

So the root cause is singular: StereoRectifier.Build is missing the actual CvInvoke.StereoRectify call that should compute R0, R1, P0, P1, and Q from the camera parameters and write them back into the calibration object before those matrices get used downstream. This one missing call explains both the NaN baseline/fx values in the logs and the complete failure to detect the ball—it's not two separate bugs, just one architectural gap in the rectification pipeline. So the bottleneck is clear now—each frame takes roughly 13-15ms to process through RectifyFrame and Detect, but the mock producer is churning out frames at 200fps per camera (400fps combined), which means the pipeline can only handle about 71fps. The consumer is falling 3-5x behind the producer.

This isn't a hang or deadlock—it's just the bounded queue filling up almost immediately and staying maxed out at 256 while the mock generator is still running. Once the 2-second mock generation window ends and production stops, the consumer finally starts draining the backlog of queued frames that accumulated during the real-time mismatch. process is happening in a single massive drain cycle that never catches up to the production rate, so only one stale detection result gets sent across the entire flight instead of continuous updates.

The real question now is why the per-frame processing itself is taking ~14ms — the stereo rectification with bilinear resampling on a 720x540 image shouldn't be that expensive on modern hardware, so there might be something else bottlenecking the pipeline.

I'm suspecting the culprit could be inefficient managed code loops doing per-pixel operations through Emgu.CV indexers, which involve interop calls for each element and are notoriously slow, or the overhead from repeatedly marshalling data across the managed/native boundary during the rectification and detection steps.

Looking at the `RectifyFrame` method, there's a nested loop iterating through all 388,800 pixels and accessing each one via the matrix indexer—that's hundreds of thousands of interop calls per frame, which would definitely tank performance. ing code comments explain this is a deliberate workaround for an Emgu.CV marshalling reliability issue, not a performance oversight. The key difference is that `BallDetector.ExtractCrop` only processes a small 48x48 region, making it negligible, whereas `RectifyFrame` iterates across the entire 720x540 frame—orders of magnitude more expensive.

The `RectifyFrame` method appears to be a recent addition tied to the stereo pipeline fix mentioned in the notes, where the rectifier was built at startup but never actually applied until now. So this performance regression is likely a genuine side effect of implementing the correctness fix—the intent was right, but the slow per-pixel Matrix indexer approach wasn't the optimal implementation choice.

Since this is blocking the smoke test entirely, I should verify the hypothesis by profiling just the Mat-to-byte-array readback versus the actual remap call to pinpoint which dominates. The faster approach would be to use a bulk copy method like `Mat.CopyTo(byte[])` instead of the current loop, similar to how other parts of the code leverage fast bulk operations. Replacing the double-loop with a direct `CopyTo(byte[])` call on the Mat object, which should be a single bulk marshal operation instead of hundreds of thousands of individual indexing operations. The comments about Marshal.Copy and KalmanFilter are specifically about writing to Mat objects, not reading from them — and since `MatToArray` already demonstrates that `CopyTo` works reliably for reading (it's the standard approach used elsewhere in the codebase), this fix is safe and follows the documented pattern. ## 2026-07-22 follow-up — four real bugs found running the mock pipeline live (not just unit tests)

Nikolas asked to smoke-test the Unity integration with `MockCameraManager` before kicking a real ball. Doing that live (`dotnet run -f net10.0-windows`) surfaced **four bugs that the 149 unit tests never caught**, because unit tests exercise each class in isolation with hand-crafted inputs — none of them ran the full camera→detect→rectify→triangulate→send pipeline together, live, with realistic timing. All four affect **real hardware operation identically**, not just the mock — this wasn't mock-only cleanup.

1. **`StereoRectifier.Build()` never actually called `CvInvoke.StereoRectify`.** It read `cal.R0/P0/R1/P1` directly and fed them to `InitUndistortRectifyMap` — but those fields are rectification *outputs* (see class comment on `StereoCalibrationData`), populated only by `StereoCalibrator.Calibrate()` for a real checkerboard run. Via `CreateDefaults()`'s fallback (no calibration file yet — see item 1 above), they were still zero, so `Triangulator.Configure` read `fx=0`/`baseline=NaN` and every 3D position came out `NaN`. Fixed: `Build()` now calls `CvInvoke.StereoRectify(K0,D0,K1,D1,imgSize,R,T,...)` itself and writes the real R0/R1/P0/P1/Q back into `cal`, mirroring what `StereoCalibrator` already did for the real-calibration path. [StereoRectifier.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoRectifier.cs)
2. **`MockCameraManager` drew a fixed 6px-radius blob (~113px² area) regardless of sport** — soccer's `MinContourArea` is 800px², so the mock ball could never pass `BallDetector`'s contour filter. Fixed: blob radius is now sized from the active profile's contour-area midpoint. [MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs)
3. **The real one, hardest to find: `SimulatorEngine.RectifyFrame`'s Mat→byte[] readback used a per-pixel `Matrix<byte>` indexer loop (388,800 individual calls) over the full 720×540 frame** — ~14ms measured per frame, slower than the ~5ms/frame budget at 200fps. The (bounded, 256-cap) frame queue backed up faster than it could drain, so an entire 2-second mock shot collapsed into one giant stale batch by the time processing caught up — `det0`/`det1` only ever reflected the *last* frame in that backlog (usually off-screen by then), so **zero or one `BallData` packet got sent per shot** instead of a live stream. `BallDetector.ExtractCrop` uses the same indexer-loop pattern safely because it only ever operates on a tiny 48×48 crop — the bug was applying that pattern to a full frame. Fixed with a direct bulk `Mat.CopyTo(byte[])` (same approach `MatToArray` already used for calibration doubles). This dropped per-frame cost from ~14ms to ~1-2ms and let real-time throughput through. Found this by adding (and then removing) stopwatch instrumentation around each pipeline stage live — worth remembering as a debugging approach if throughput problems show up again with real hardware. [SimulatorEngine.cs](../App/SimulatorEngine.cs)
4. **`StereoCalibrationData.CreateDefaults()`'s `T` (stereo translation vector) had the wrong sign.** OpenCV's convention is `X_cam1 = R·X_cam0 + T`; for camera1 (right) sitting physically further +X than camera0 (left), `T`'s X component must be *negative* — `CreateDefaults` had it positive, which (combined with `Triangulator`'s correct, standard `baseline = -P1[0,3]/P1[0,0]` formula) made every computed baseline come out negative, which made every real-stereo Z land outside the sane `[0.05m, 10m]` range, which silently self-demoted `TriangulateStereo` to its internal `Monocular()` fallback — which hardcodes `X=Y=Z=0`. So even *after* fixing bug #1 and #3, every ball position reported was exactly `(0,0,0)`. Fixed by negating `T` in `CreateDefaults`; updated the two `StereoCalibrationDataTests` that had asserted the (wrong) positive sign as their contract. [StereoCalibrationData.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrationData.cs)

**After all four fixes**, a live mock run produces genuinely correct output: `[Triangulator] Baseline: 495.3mm  fx: 1757.7px` (was `NaNmm  0.0px`), and `[Ball]` lines show a real, physically sensible trajectory (Z increasing as the ball flies away, Y rising then falling under gravity, `tier=FullStereo` with conf≈0.94 during the stereo-agreement window). All 149 tests still pass.

**Not yet re-validated against Unity itself** — this confirmed the middleware's own pipeline now produces real `BallData`, but the actual UDP send → `UdpReceiverNew` → `BallController` hop (see item 4 in "Still open" above) hasn't been re-tested live since these fixes landed.

It's the model, not your Unity scripts — and I can point to exactly why.

`KalmanBallTracker.Configure()` hardcodes `dt = 1/199.76f` (≈5ms) into its transition matrix, and assumes every single `Update()`/`Predict()` call corresponds to exactly one camera tick at that rate:

```csharp
float dt = 1f / 199.76f;
SetMatrix(_kf.TransitionMatrix, new float[,] { {1,0,0,dt,0,0}, ... });
```

But `SimulatorEngine.ProcessLoop()` calls `_tracker.Update(...)`/`_tracker.Predict()` **once per outer loop cycle**, not once per frame — and each cycle can drain a variable number of frames (I saw `drain=2` up to `drain=20` in testing) depending on processing load at that instant. So the real elapsed time between successive Kalman calls is often several times longer than the ~5ms the filter assumes. Since neither `Update()` nor `Predict()` is ever given the frame's actual `TimestampUs`, the filter has no way to correct for that — it just silently attributes each real position jump to a much shorter time window than actually passed, which systematically drags the recovered velocity down. That lines up with what you saw: the mock's real launch speed is 30 m/s, but the diagnostic run I did earlier showed the tracker reporting only ~3.1 m/s — roughly the same ballpark of underestimate you'd expect from that timing mismatch. A weak velocity handed to Unity means `BallController` (which now drives the Rigidbody directly off that real m/s value) launches the ball far too slowly to reach the net.

This is a real architecture bug in the middleware, not mock-specific — it'd bias speed on real hardware too, any time processing falls even slightly behind camera rate.

The fix: have `KalmanBallTracker.Update`/`Predict` take the frame's actual timestamp, compute real elapsed `dt` from the previous call, and rebuild the dt-dependent transition matrix entries each time instead of using a fixed constant. Want me to implement that?

content.text:
## Summary

Root-caused and fixed. Two more real bugs, on top of the earlier ones:

1. **`KalmanBallTracker` hardcoded a fixed `dt=1/199.76`** into its velocity model, assuming every call happens exactly one camera-tick apart. It doesn't — `ProcessLoop` batches a variable number of frames per cycle, so real elapsed time routinely exceeded that assumption, systematically underestimating velocity. Fixed by threading the frame's real `TimestampUs` through `Update`/`Predict` and rebuilding the transition matrix from actual elapsed time each call.

2. **The real blocker: `MockCameraManager` was silently simulating a different camera than the one your calibration assumes** — 1280×1024 @ fx=1800, versus `StereoCalibrationData`'s real 720×540 @ fx≈1757.7 (confirmed on-site). Nothing threw on this mismatch — it just made the rectifier's remap sample from the wrong place, washing out real disparity from an expected ~290px down to ~4-5px. That's why every stereo triangulation attempt was self-rejecting. Fixed by exposing the real camera model as shared constants on `StereoCalibrationData` and having the mock reference them directly instead of an independently-drifting copy.

I also adjusted the mock's starting distance (~3m, matching your rig) and default trajectory (12 m/s / 8°, a realistic captured-near-the-tee shot rather than a 30 m/s drive that flies past the practical tracking range).

**Result**: a live run now shows sustained `tier=FullStereo` with confidence 0.92-0.94, and speed climbing correctly toward the true trajectory value (3.2→5.1→6.1→6.5→7.0 m/s converging toward 12 m/s truth) as real measurements accumulate — genuine convergence, not a stuck wrong value. All 149 tests pass.

One thing worth watching: full convergence to the *exact* true speed takes more measurements than a short capture window provides — that's an inherent property of this Kalman tuning (existing test comments already note "200-400 frames to reach steady state"), not a new bug. If the ball still feels underpowered in Unity, that's the next thing to look at (e.g., seeding initial velocity from the first two measurements instead of zero) — but worth testing live first to see if it's actually a problem in practice now.

Documented everything in [14-session-2026-07-22-hardware-bringup.md](notes/14-session-2026-07-22-hardware-bringup.md). Give it another run in Unity when you get a chance.

Implemented, and I want to be straight about the results — it's a real but partial improvement, not a full fix.

**What I did:**
1. `KalmanBallTracker` now holds the first real measurement and seeds velocity from the position delta to the second, instead of starting at zero.
2. While testing that, I found it was actually getting **poisoned**: `SimulatorEngine`'s single-camera (Tier 3) fallback uses the tracker's own last-known Z as a depth reference — before any real stereo fix exists, that's 0, so an early Tier 3 detection (common, since one camera's background model warms up before the other's) fed a garbage `(0,0,0)`-ish point into the seed. Fixed by gating Tier 3 behind `HasFix` — it now coasts instead of using a fabricated depth until a genuine stereo measurement lands first.

**Live result at 18 m/s across a few runs**: first reported speed ranged 5.7–10.4 m/s (was 3.1–5.9 before this change) — better, but with real run-to-run variance, and still short of the true 18 m/s within the ball's brief time inside stereo range. All 149 tests pass (one test's assertion needed updating to reflect the new fast-converge behavior instead of the old slow-climb behavior).

**Why it's not fully converged**: two-point seeding trades "instant estimate" for "noise sensitivity" — if the two seed measurements happen to land close together in time, small position-detection noise (± a couple pixels) gets divided by a small Δt, amplifying into real velocity error. That's a known tradeoff of raw two-point estimation, not a bug.

Set the mock back to 18 m/s (matching what you asked me to test) — build's clean, tests pass. If you want tighter accuracy, the natural next step is fitting velocity across the first several measurements (least-squares) instead of just two raw points, or retuning `ProcessNoise`/`MeasurementNoise`. But it's worth testing this in Unity first — the numeric undershoot may matter less in practice once Unity's own physics takes over the flight.

content.thinking:
The user is asking a sharp question about why simple distance-over-time calculations don't give accurate speed measurements. The core issue is that while the formula itself is exact, the real-world measurements feeding into it—particularly position estimates from stereo triangulation—contain noise and error, and that measurement uncertainty in the distance component is what degrades the final speed calculation.

Each detected position comes from noisy pixel measurements that get triangulated into 3D space, and that triangulation error scales with depth in a predictable way: a pixel or two of detection noise translates to centimeter-level position uncertainty at typical working distances. When I compute velocity as the change in position over time, I'm differencing two noisy measurements, and that noise compounds the problem—even small independent errors in consecutive position estimates can create significant velocity noise.

The real issue is that I'm trying to estimate velocity from measurements separated by only 5-10ms, which is a tiny time window. Over that interval, the actual displacement is only 5-18cm at typical speeds, but the position noise alone is 2-3cm per measurement. When those errors combine across two independent samples, the displacement estimate itself becomes noisy by 3-4cm—which is 20-70% of the true signal. This is the classic numerical differentiation trap: dividing a small, noisy difference by a small time interval amplifies the noise relative to the true signal.

I could try waiting longer between measurements to get more displacement relative to the noise floor, but that creates two problems. First, over a longer time window the trajectory curves due to gravity and drag, so it's no longer truly instantaneous. Second, and more practically, I don't have the freedom to choose an arbitrarily long baseline for the initial velocity measurements.

The real constraint is that I want the earliest possible velocity estimate within the brief capture window, and if I delay too long waiting for a second point, I've already burned through valuable tracking time before reporting anything. So the two-point approach is physically sound in principle, but it's inherently noise-sensitive because it relies on just two samples with real detection noise, and the frame-to-frame time interval (limited by camera frame rate, around 5ms) is small relative to the position measurement noise at this range.

The solution that launch monitors actually use is to avoid relying on just two raw points. Instead, I should use more measurements—maybe the first 5-10 real position fixes—and fit a line through them using least-squares regression to average out the noise. The real issue is that dividing a noisy small displacement by a small time interval magnifies the noise in the velocity estimate — a classic numerical differentiation problem. I should fit a least-squares line across multiple points instead of just using a raw two-point difference. To make this concrete, I'll pull actual numbers from the MockCameraManager's noise model — the 1.5-pixel Gaussian noise added to each camera's raw detection — and show how that propagates through to the velocity calculation with real, verifiable figures from this specific system.

The centroid calculation itself might introduce minor computational noise, but the dominant source is the 1.5-pixel Gaussian noise per camera. When triangulating depth via disparity, both cameras' pixel noise combine independently, giving a disparity noise of roughly 2.12 pixels. The sensitivity of depth to disparity changes follows dZ/d(disparity) = −Z²/(fx·baseline), so at 5 meters I can compute exactly how much depth noise that produces.

At the actual camera parameters (Z=5m, fx≈1757.7, baseline≈0.495m), the disparity noise of 2.12 pixels translates to about 6.1 centimeters of depth noise per stereo measurement. But over a single 5-millisecond frame interval at 18 m/s, the true depth displacement is only 9 centimeters. This means the measurement noise is nearly as large as the actual motion signal itself—that's why two-point velocity estimates are so unreliable with this sensor configuration.

I should also verify the lateral position noise: at Z=5m, pixel noise of 1.5 pixels gives roughly 4.3 millimeters of X/Y error, which is much smaller than the depth noise. This asymmetry makes sense because depth comes from disparity (a subtraction of two noisy measurements with a nonlinear 1/disparity relationship), while X/Y scale linearly with pixel error. the path forward is either fitting a least-squares line across multiple frames to smooth out the noise, or explicitly accounting for the fact that depth measurements are inherently noisier in stereo systems. content.text:
Good question — the physics (speed = distance/time) is exactly right, and `time` is measured essentially perfectly (real frame timestamps). The problem is `distance`: it's not measured directly, it's *triangulated* from noisy pixel detections, and dividing a noisy displacement by a tiny time interval amplifies that noise dramatically. Let me show you with the actual numbers from your system.

`MockCameraManager` adds ~1.5px of Gaussian noise to each camera's detected ball position (`_positionNoisePx = 1.5f`) — modeling real detector jitter. Depth (Z) in stereo vision comes from **disparity** (the difference between the two cameras' pixel positions), and depth error scales with `Z²/(fx·baseline)` — this formula is already in your code (`Triangulator.DepthPrecisionMm`). At Z=5m:

```
depth noise ≈ (5² / (1757.7 × 0.4953)) × ~2.1px combined pixel noise ≈ 6cm
```

Now compare that to how far the ball *actually* moves between two successive frames at 18 m/s, ~5ms apart:

```
true displacement ≈ 18 × 0.005 = 9cm
```

**The noise (~6cm) is almost as large as the signal (~9cm).** That's why two-point seeding is so unstable — you're not dividing a clean distance by time, you're dividing "9cm ± 6cm" by 5ms. A single bad pixel detection swings the computed velocity wildly.

Two things make this specifically bad for this rig:
1. **Depth is the noisiest axis in any stereo system** — X/Y come from a single camera's pixel position scaled by `Z/fx` (much more direct, ~4mm of noise at this range), but Z comes from *subtracting* two already-noisy numbers (disparity), which amplifies error. That's just how triangulation works, not a bug.
2. **The ball's motion here is mostly along Z** (flying away from the camera) — so the noisiest measurement axis is also the dominant direction of true motion, which is the worst-case combination.

The fix that actually addresses this: don't take a velocity from just 2 points — fit a line (least-squares) through the first 5-10 real position measurements instead. Independent per-point noise averages out roughly by `√N`, so 8 points would cut the noise's effect by more than half versus 2 points, while still converging in a handful of frames rather than hundreds. Want me to implement that instead of the raw two-point delta?

content.text:
All three runs now stay well within a plausible range (2–1294 rpm) — no more of the 5000-6000rpm spikes that were driving the orbit. That said, since the mock doesn't actually model spin, the "true" answer is 0, and you'll still see occasional non-zero noise up to the 1500rpm cap — this is a safety ceiling, not a perfect fix. The real validation of spin accuracy still needs a real textured ball on real hardware, exactly as the code's own comments already flagged.

Summary of what changed:
1. **Velocity seeding**: replaced the noise-sensitive two-point delta with a least-squares line fit through the first 8 real measurements — averages out detection noise instead of amplifying it.
2. **Mock ball texture**: added fixed internal speckles so `FeaturePointTracker` has real (if imperfect) features to track, instead of pure edge noise.
3. **Spin plausibility clamp**: reject any `Spin3DEstimator` reading above 1500rpm (no in-scope sport goes anywhere near that) — this is what actually kills the orbiting, since it stops physically-impossible readings from ever reaching `BallController`'s Magnus force calculation.

All 149 tests pass. Give it another run in Unity — the orbiting should be gone. If you still see meaningful curve at the higher end of that range (1000+ rpm), let me know and I can lower the cap further or just disable spin output entirely for mock testing.

85	Nikolas ran the fixed mock pipeline end-to-end into Unity: the ball moved, but never reached the net. Root-caused to two further bugs (found by adding, then removing, live instrumentation — Console.WriteLine per frame is itself slow enough to distort the timing being measured, a real observer-effect trap; cheap in-memory counters printed only on the existing throttled log line were the reliable way to see what was actually happening without changing it).
86	
87	1. **`KalmanBallTracker` hardcoded `dt = 1/199.76f` into its transition matrix**, assuming every `Update()`/`Predict()` call corresponds to exactly one camera tick. It doesn't — `SimulatorEngine.ProcessLoop` batches a variable number of frames per cycle (observed `drain=2` up to `drain=20` depending on processing load at that instant), so the real elapsed time between tracker calls routinely exceeded the assumed ~5ms by a wide margin. That silently and systematically underestimated recovered velocity. Fixed: `Update`/`Predict` now take the frame's actual `TimestampUs`, and the transition matrix's dt is rebuilt each call from the real elapsed time since the previous one (clamped `[1e-4s, 0.5s]` against duplicate timestamps / long coasts). Updated `KalmanTrackerTests.cs`/`KalmanTrackerAdditionalTests.cs` to pass explicit timestamps matching their own `dt` variables. [KalmanBallTracker.cs](../Tracking/KalmanBallTracker.cs)
88	2. **The real remaining blocker: `MockCameraManager` silently modeled a completely different camera than the one `StereoCalibrationData.CreateDefaults()` (and therefore `StereoRectifier`/`Triangulator`) assumes.** Mock generated 1280×1024 frames at fx=1800 (stale numbers, predating the on-site confirmation of the real camera's specs); `CreateDefaults()` builds a 720×540/fx≈1757.7 model. Nothing throws on this mismatch — it just makes `StereoRectifier`'s remap tables sample from the wrong place, which **washed out real disparity almost entirely**: true disparity at working distance should be ~290px, but detected (post-rectify) disparity measured only ~4-5px. That's why `TriangulateStereo` self-rejected on every single attempt (disparity too small even to clear the `disparity <= 0.5f` "behind baseline" guard, some of the time) — not a range or sign issue this time, the two cameras' images had been rectified into near-agreement with each other, destroying the very depth cue triangulation needs. Fixed by exposing the real camera model's constants as `public const`/`static` members on `StereoCalibrationData` (`DefaultImageWidth/Height`, `DefaultFx`) and having `MockCameraManager` reference them directly instead of maintaining an independent, silently-driftable copy. Also updated `MockCameraManagerTests.cs`'s hardcoded `1280×1024` assertions to reference the same constants. [MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs), [StereoCalibrationData.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrationData.cs)

90	Also, while chasing this, found the mock's default ball-start position (0.5m from camera) and default trajectory (30 m/s / 15°, a full-power drive-distance kick) put most of a shot's flight either deep inside `Triangulator`'s close-range zone or past its 10m far-range cutoff — nowhere near the real rig's confirmed ~3m working distance. `Program.cs`'s mock setup now starts the ball at ~3m (`MockCameraManager.BallStartZ`) and uses a more modest 12 m/s / 8° trajectory representative of a shot actually captured near the tee, with Unity's own local physics (`BallController`) carrying the rest of the flight — matching the intended "brief burst capture near the tee, not a full continuous track" design in [11-unity-integration.md](11-unity-integration.md).
91

[MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs), [StereoCalibrationData.cs](../Vision/Calibration/StereoCalibrationData.cs)

Also, while chasing this, found the mock's default ball-start position (0.5m from camera) and default trajectory (30 m/s / 15°, a full-power drive-distance kick) put most of a shot's flight either deep inside `Triangulator`'s close-range zone or past its 10m far-range cutoff — nowhere near the real rig's confirmed ~3m working distance. `Program.cs`'s mock setup now starts the ball at ~3m (`MockCameraManager.BallStartZ`) and uses a more modest 12 m/s / 8° trajectory representative of a shot actually captured near the tee, with Unity's own local physics (`BallController`) carrying the rest of the flight — matching the intended "brief burst capture near the tee, not a full continuous track" design in [11-unity-integration.md](11-unity-integration.md).

**After both fixes**, a live run shows sustained `tier=FullStereo` (not a 2-cycle fluke), confidence 0.92–0.94, and speed climbing correctly toward the true trajectory value across successive real measurements (observed 3.2→5.1→6.1→6.5→7.0 m/s converging toward the 12 m/s truth) — genuine Kalman convergence from its zero-velocity prior, not a stuck/wrong steady-state. **Still open**: full convergence to the exact true speed takes more real measurements than a very short capture window provides (the existing `KalmanTrackerTests.cs` comment already notes "typically 200-400 frames to reach steady state" for this filter/tuning) — worth watching whether reported speed is close enough for a satisfying Unity shot, or whether the filter needs faster-converging tuning (e.g. seeding initial velocity from the first two measurements instead of zero) if it's consistently undershooting in practice. ## 2026-07-22 third follow-up — velocity seeding, spin noise, and a mid-shot reset bug

At 18 m/s the previous fix's two-point velocity seed proved noise-sensitive: dividing a small noisy displacement (stereo depth noise ≈6cm at Z=5m, per `Triangulator.DepthPrecisionMm`) by a small dt (~5ms, ~9cm of true displacement at 18 m/s) amplifies detection noise into a wildly inaccurate velocity — worse the shorter the gap between the two seed points. Replaced with a least-squares line fit (position vs. time, independently per axis) through the first 8 real measurements (`KalmanBallTracker.SeedFromBuffer`) — averages out independent per-measurement noise roughly by `√N` instead of amplifying it. `KalmanTrackerTests.cs` updated (some tests only fed 2 measurements, matching the old design).

Separately, Nikolas reported the ball orbiting in a circle before reaching the net — traced to `[Spin3D]` readings swinging wildly frame to frame (single digits to 5000+ rpm). Root cause: `MockCameraManager`'s ball was a perfectly flat white disc with zero internal texture, so `FeaturePointTracker`'s GFTT corner detector was tracking edge/threshold noise, not real features — and `BallController` applies that spin directly as a Magnus force, so one bad ~5000rpm reading with a near-vertical axis was enough to send the ball into a sustained curve. Added fixed internal speckles to the mock ball (`MockCameraManager._speckleOffsets`, never rotated — matching the physical truth that this mock doesn't model spin at all) so the tracker has real points to find; this alone wasn't sufficient (still saw occasional 5000+ rpm — visually-identical speckles are genuinely ambiguous for `FindStereoMatch`'s cross-camera template matching, unlike a real ball's locally-distinctive seams/panels). Added a direct plausibility guard in `Spin3DEstimator.Estimate`: reject any reading above 1500rpm (well beyond any in-scope sport's real range — golf's much higher real spin is out of scope) rather than feed a physically-impossible value into the Magnus force. This is what actually stops the orbiting; the speckle texture is a secondary improvement, not a full fix — true spin accuracy validation still needs a real textured ball on real hardware.

Then: "why is it sending multiple shots?" — it wasn't. `[Ball] speed=15.2m/s` two lines later becomes `speed=0.0m/s` — the tracker's converged velocity got wiped mid-flight. Cause: Unity's `ProfileSelectSender` resends `"soccer"` up to 5 times over ~8s after Play (no ack in this protocol, so it can't know if the first one landed — see notes above on retry behavior). Every resend, even for an already-active profile, went through `SimulatorEngine.OnProfileCommand` → `ApplyProfile` → `KalmanBallTracker.Configure()`, which builds a **brand new** `KalmanFilter` from scratch. Since the mock's 2-second shot fires within that same retry window, a redundant resend landing mid-flight silently reset tracking to zero. This is a real bug for any deployment, not mock-specific — I'd flagged the theoretical risk earlier in this session but hadn't yet seen it actually bite. Fixed: `OnProfileCommand` now short-circuits (`return`, no reset) if the requested `SportId` already matches `_activeProfile.SportId` — switching profiles still resets state when the sport actually changes, but redundant re-selection of the same sport is now a true no-op. All 149 tests pass throughout.

content.text:
## Summary

That wasn't multiple shots — it was one shot getting its tracking silently reset mid-flight. `speed=15.2m/s` dropping to `speed=0.0m/s` two lines later was the tell.

**Root cause**: Unity's `ProfileSelectSender` resends `"soccer"` up to 5 times over ~8 seconds after Play (since there's no ack in this protocol, it can't tell if the first one landed). Every one of those resends — even though the sport hasn't actually changed — went through `SimulatorEngine.OnProfileCommand` → `ApplyProfile` → `KalmanBallTracker.Configure()`, which builds a **brand-new Kalman filter from scratch**, discarding whatever velocity it had converged on. Since the mock's shot fires within that same retry window, one of the redundant resends landed mid-flight and wiped tracking back to zero.

This is a real bug for the actual deployed scenario too, not just mock testing — I'd flagged the theoretical risk earlier in this conversation but hadn't seen it actually happen until now.

**Fix**: `OnProfileCommand` now checks if the requested sport already matches the active one, and skips the reset entirely if so — switching sports still resets state when it actually changes, but re-selecting the same sport is now a true no-op.

Also implemented the least-squares velocity fit you asked for, and (separately) tracked down the orbiting: the mock ball's flat texture-less surface produced wildly noisy spin readings that fed directly into the Magnus force. Added a plausibility cap (1500rpm — well beyond any in-scope sport) that's what actually stops the orbiting; I also gave the mock ball some fixed internal texture but that alone wasn't sufficient (identical-looking speckles still confuse stereo point-matching). All 149 tests pass, documented in the notes. Worth another Unity run — the velocity should hold steady through the whole flight now instead of resetting partway through.

Looking at the two ball position readings, I can see a significant shift in both location and spin characteristics—the position moved from near the origin to much further downfield, the speed increased slightly, and the spin rate jumped dramatically from 25 to 95 rpm while the confidence dropped from 0.94 to 0.56, suggesting the trajectory did change but the second measurement is less reliable. The earlier spin measurements were actually below my 1500rpm rejection threshold, so they got accepted as valid despite their high values and constantly flipping axes between +Y and -Y directions. Since these spins are being applied to the ball in Unity, they're likely causing the Magnus force effects that are distorting the trajectory, even though the individual spin values seem plausible on their own. accepted and passed to Unity's BallController, which then applies dramatically shifting Magnus forces between frames as the spin axis flips between +Y and -Y — this rapid reversal of force direction would absolutely create that visible mid-flight trajectory change. So the 1500rpm threshold I set isn't actually filtering out the noise effectively; values like 1474, 1165, and 1110 are still slipping through and causing real artifacts.

The real issue is that soccer spin should only be in the 300-600rpm range according to the codebase itself, so anything above that is already suspect — but rather than just raising the magnitude cap higher, I should add a consistency check that flags and rejects large swings or axis reversals between consecutive readings, since those are clearly spurious noise rather than realistic ball physics.

To directly answer the user: yes, the logs do show a plausible mechanism for the mid-air trajectory shift, but it's through spin fluctuations rather than a speed reset — the spin values jumped around significantly (hitting 1474, 1165, 1110 rpm) which are all well above what real soccer physics would produce, and those noise artifacts are likely what's causing the visual perturbations.

The fix should be more aggressive: either lower the spin cap substantially (maybe to 700 rpm to match documented real-world ranges) or better yet, reject large frame-to-frame changes in spin values rather than just capping the magnitude, since 1500 rpm clearly wasn't a tight enough threshold. The practical fix would be to cap the spin plausibility at a lower threshold, around 700 rpm, to match real-world soccer physics where spin rarely exceeds 600 rpm. [Spin3D] rpm=1474 axis=(-0.08,0.99,0.11)   ← strong +Y axis spin

These readings are all **under my 1500rpm cap**, so they weren't rejected — they went straight through as real spin, and `BallController.ApplyHit` overwrites the ball's Magnus-force spin vector on every single packet it receives. A sequence like that — strong sideways curl force, then reversed, then reversed again, all within a fraction of a second of real flight — is exactly what a visible "kink" or sudden direction change mid-air would look like. It's not a new bug, it's the same root problem (no real texture to measure spin from) slipping past a cap that wasn't tight enough: soccer's real documented spin range in this codebase is ~300-600rpm, so anything over ~1000 is already obviously noise, and my 1500 ceiling let it through.

Let me tighten that cap.

content.text:
All 149 tests pass with the tightened cap (700rpm). To directly answer your question:

**Yes, the logs confirm it — and it's not a new bug, it's the same spin-noise issue slipping past the cap I set too loosely.**

Speed itself was fine (16.1→16.5 m/s, no reset — that fix held). But look at the full `[Spin3D]` stream between your two `[Ball]` snapshots:

```
rpm=1474 axis=(-0.08, 0.99, 0.11)   ← strong spin, +Y axis
rpm=1165 axis=(0.36, -0.93, 0.08)   ← similar magnitude, axis flipped to -Y
rpm=1110 axis=(-0.40, 0.91, -0.08)  ← flipped back to +Y
```

All three were under my 1500rpm cap, so none got rejected — they went straight to `BallController`, which applies whatever spin vector arrives as a real Magnus (curve) force on every packet. A strong sideways force that reverses direction twice within a fraction of a second is exactly what a visible mid-air kink looks like. It's not new physics going wrong, it's the same "mock ball has no real texture, so spin readings are noise" problem — my cap just wasn't tight enough to catch this particular range of noise.

I've tightened it from 1500 → 700rpm, right at soccer's real documented ceiling (~600rpm) with a little headroom, which would have rejected all three of those readings. Build's clean, all 149 tests pass.

Worth knowing going in: this cap is a blunt instrument — it stops the worst artifacts but doesn't make spin *accurate*, since the mock still has no way to produce a real signal. If you see another kink at a lower magnitude, that's this same limitation, not a new bug. The actual fix for spin accuracy is a real textured ball on real hardware, same as the code's own comments have said from the start.

## 2026-07-22 fourth follow-up — root-caused the remaining velocity instability, verified against real camera specs

Nikolas correctly pushed back on an assumption: I'd been treating `MockCameraManager`'s injected `_positionNoisePx = 1.5f` detection noise as roughly realistic. He supplied the actual Blackfly S BFS-PGE-04S2M-CS spec sheet (720×540, 6.9μm pixel pitch, Sony IMX287 global shutter) — resolution matched what `StereoCalibrationData.CreateDefaults()` already models, confirming that part was solid. But the noise figure wasn't really about camera optics at all — it was about how precisely `BallDetector` locates the ball within that pixel grid, which is a software question. Checked `BallDetector.Detect()` and found it was computing the center from `CvInvoke.BoundingRectangle` — `rect.X + rect.Width/2f`, both integers, so the reported center can only ever land on half-pixel increments. That's real, avoidable imprecision, not a hardware limit. Replaced it with an image-moment centroid (`CvInvoke.Moments` → `M10/M00, M01/M00`), the standard technique for genuine sub-pixel accuracy (~0.1–0.3px on a clean, well-contrasted blob this size) — benefits real hardware too, not just the mock. Reduced `MockCameraManager._positionNoisePx` from 1.5px to 0.3px to match what this improved detector can actually achieve, instead of modeling noise sized for the coarse method it no longer uses. [BallDetector.cs](../Vision/BallDetector.cs), [MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs)

Spin got noticeably calmer after this (no more 1000+rpm swings), but reported speed was still unstable — worse, it now swung in *both* directions run to run (one run seeded at 33.8m/s against an 18m/s truth, another at 2.8-6m/s), and once seeded, the filter wasn't correcting back toward the truth even after many subsequent real measurements. Added a one-shot diagnostic print inside `KalmanBallTracker.SeedFromBuffer` and found the real cause: **every single one of the 8 buffered seed measurements was exactly `(0.000, 0.000, 0.000)`.** This was the same self-referential bootstrapping bug already fixed for Tier 3 (see the third follow-up above — `TriangulateMonocular` needs an existing Z reference, and before any real fix, that reference is a meaningless 0) — but present in a *different*, ungated code path: when `TriangulateStereo` itself self-rejects internally (returns its hardcoded `(0,0,0)` Monocular fallback), `SimulatorEngine`'s "enrich with the Kalman's last Z" logic was *also* using `_tracker.LastState.z`, which is equally meaningless before `HasFix` is true. The `HasFix` guard I'd added earlier only covered the Tier 3 branch, not this Tier 1-self-reject-then-enrich branch. Fixed by applying the same `HasFix` check there: before a real fix exists, a self-rejected stereo attempt now coasts (`TriangulationTier.KalmanOnly`, routed to `Predict()` not `Update()`) instead of feeding a fabricated zero into the seed buffer.

**After this fix**, four consecutive live runs at the 18 m/s test trajectory all converged to **19-20 m/s** — no more run-to-run variance between 2.8 and 33.8, no more decay after seeding, stable through the whole tracked flight. This was very likely the dominant remaining cause of "the ball changes direction/speed unpredictably" — the earlier fixes (dt, least-squares seeding, sub-pixel centroid, spin cap) were all real and necessary, but this bootstrapping bug was corrupting the seed's actual input data regardless of how good the fitting math on top of it was. All 149 tests pass throughout.

## Summary

Found the real root cause of the instability, and it's a good validation of your pushback on the noise numbers.

**Camera specs checked out** — 720×540, 6.9μm pixel pitch — matches what the calibration already models. But the 1.5px noise assumption was measuring the wrong thing: `BallDetector` was computing the ball's center from `CvInvoke.BoundingRectangle` (`rect.X + rect.Width/2f`), which only ever lands on half-pixel increments since both are integers. Replaced it with a proper image-moment centroid — the standard sub-pixel technique — and reduced the mock's noise from 1.5px to 0.3px to match. This improves real hardware too, not just the mock.

That made spin much calmer, but speed was *still* unstable — actually worse in a new way, swinging between 2.8 and 33.8 m/s run to run against an 18 m/s truth, and never correcting back after seeding. I added one diagnostic print and found it directly: **every one of the 8 measurements feeding the velocity seed was exactly `(0.000, 0.000, 0.000)`.** Same bug class as the Tier 3 fix from earlier in this conversation — `TriangulateMonocular` needs a real prior Z, and before any fix exists that's meaningless — but in a different code path: when `TriangulateStereo` self-rejects internally, `SimulatorEngine`'s "enrich with the Kalman's last Z" logic was using that same meaningless 0. Fixed by gating it with the same `HasFix` check.

**Result**: four consecutive runs at 18 m/s all converged to 19-20 m/s, stable through the whole flight, no more wild swings. This was very likely the dominant cause of the erratic direction/speed changes you'd been seeing — everything else (dt fix, least-squares seeding, sub-pixel centroid, spin cap) was real and necessary, but this bug was corrupting the actual input data underneath all of it. All 149 tests pass. Give it another run in Unity — this should be a real, stable shot now.
