content.text:
That confirms the diagnosis I flagged earlier but only partially addressed: tightening the magnitude cap stopped the extreme spikes, but it can't fix an **axis that's still essentially random every reading**. Look at this shot's axis sequence:

```
(-0.87, 0.46, 0.14) → (-0.06, 1.00,-0.01) → (-0.97, 0.19, 0.15) → (0.56,-0.80, 0.21) → (0.98, 0.20,-0.08) → ...
```

None of these individually breaks the 700rpm cap, so none get rejected — but the direction keeps flipping essentially randomly. Here's the part that matters for what you're seeing: `BallController.ApplyHit` *overwrites* the ball's spin vector completely on **every single packet it receives** — and the middleware sends far more packets per second than the throttled `[Ball]` log shows (that's only every 20th one). So Unity isn't getting one moderate, fixed spin value — it's getting dozens of different spin vectors per second, each nudging the Magnus force in a different direction. Individually plausible, collectively it reads as erratic, jittery curving — which is exactly "curving weirdly," not a clean, consistent curve.

At this point I think we've exhausted the reasonable fixes for making Spin3D's *signal* trustworthy on synthetic mock data — better texture, magnitude caps, sub-pixel centroid — the axis itself has no real information in it because the mock doesn't model actual ball rotation. Continuing to patch thresholds is chasing a ceiling that keeps needing to move.

The direct fix: disable spin output entirely when running via `MockCameraManager`, so Unity gets a clean trajectory with `SpinRpm=0` during mock testing, and only re-enable it once you're on real hardware with an actual textured ball where Spin3D has something real to measure. Want me to do that?

102	## 2026-07-22 fourth follow-up — root-caused the remaining velocity instability, verified against real camera specs
103	
104	Nikolas correctly pushed back on an assumption: I'd been treating `MockCameraManager`'s injected `_positionNoisePx = 1.5f` detection noise as roughly realistic. He supplied the actual Blackfly S BFS-PGE-04S2M-CS spec sheet (720×540, 6.9μm pixel pitch, Sony IMX287 global shutter) — resolution matched what `StereoCalibrationData.CreateDefaults()` already models, confirming that part was solid. But the noise figure wasn't really about camera optics at all — it was about how precisely `BallDetector` locates the ball within that pixel grid, which is a software question. Checked `BallDetector.Detect()` and found it was computing the center from `CvInvoke.BoundingRectangle` — `rect.X + rect.Width/2f`, both integers, so the reported center can only ever land on half-pixel increments. That's real, avoidable imprecision, not a hardware limit. Replaced it with an image-moment centroid (`CvInvoke.Moments` → `M10/M00, M01/M00`), the standard technique for genuine sub-pixel accuracy (~0.1–0.3px on a clean, well-contrasted blob this size) — benefits real hardware too, not just the mock. Reduced `MockCameraManager._positionNoisePx` from 1.5px to 0.3px to match what this improved detector can actually achieve, instead of modeling noise sized for the coarse method it no longer uses. [BallDetector.cs](../Vision/BallDetector.cs), [MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs)
105	
106	Spin got noticeably calmer after this (no more 1000+rpm swings), but reported speed was still unstable — worse, it now swung in *both* directions run to run (one run seeded at 33.8m/s against an 18m/s truth, another at 2.8-6m/s), and once seeded, the filter wasn't correcting back toward the truth even after many subsequent real measurements. Added a one-shot diagnostic print inside `KalmanBallTracker.SeedFromBuffer` and found the real cause: **every single one of the 8 buffered seed measurements was exactly `(0.000, 0.000, 0.000)`.** This was the same self-referential bootstrapping bug already fixed for Tier 3 (see the third follow-up above — `TriangulateMonocular` needs an existing Z reference, and before any real fix, that reference is a meaningless 0) — but present in a *different*, ungated code path: when `TriangulateStereo` itself self-rejects internally (returns its hardcoded `(0,0,0)` Monocular fallback), `SimulatorEngine`'s "enrich with the Kalman's last Z" logic was *also* using `_tracker.LastState.z`, which is equally meaningless before `HasFix` is true. The `HasFix` guard I'd added earlier only covered the Tier 3 branch, not this Tier 1-self-reject-then-enrich branch. Fixed by applying the same `HasFix` check there: before a real fix exists, a self-rejected stereo attempt now coasts (`TriangulationTier.KalmanOnly`, routed to `Predict()` not `Update()`) instead of feeding a fabricated zero into the seed buffer.
107	
108	**After this fix**, four consecutive live runs at the 18 m/s test trajectory all converged to **19-20 m/s** — no more run-to-run variance between 2.8 and 33.8, no more decay after seeding, stable through the whole tracked flight. This was very likely the dominant remaining cause of "the ball changes direction/speed unpredictably" — the earlier fixes (dt, least-squares seeding, sub-pixel centroid, spin cap) were all real and necessary, but this bootstrapping bug was corrupting the seed's actual input data regardless of how good the fitting math on top of it was. ## 2026-07-22 fourth follow-up — root-caused the remaining velocity instability, verified against real camera specs

Nikolas correctly pushed back on an assumption: I'd been treating `MockCameraManager`'s injected `_positionNoisePx = 1.5f` detection noise as roughly realistic. He supplied the actual Blackfly S BFS-PGE-04S2M-CS spec sheet (720×540, 6.9μm pixel pitch, Sony IMX287 global shutter) — resolution matched what `StereoCalibrationData.CreateDefaults()` already models, confirming that part was solid. But the noise figure wasn't really about camera optics at all — it was about how precisely `BallDetector` locates the ball within that pixel grid, which is a software question. Checked `BallDetector.Detect()` and found it was computing the center from `CvInvoke.BoundingRectangle` — `rect.X + rect.Width/2f`, both integers, so the reported center can only ever land on half-pixel increments. That's real, avoidable imprecision, not a hardware limit. Replaced it with an image-moment centroid (`CvInvoke.Moments` → `M10/M00, M01/M00`), the standard technique for genuine sub-pixel accuracy (~0.1–0.3px on a clean, well-contrasted blob this size) — benefits real hardware too, not just the mock. Reduced `MockCameraManager._positionNoisePx` from 1.5px to 0.3px to match what this improved detector can actually achieve, instead of modeling noise sized for the coarse method it no longer uses. [BallDetector.cs](../Vision/BallDetector.cs), [MockCameraManager.cs](../Vision/MockCameraManager.cs)

Spin got noticeably calmer after this (no more 1000+rpm swings), but reported speed was still unstable — worse, it now swung in *both* directions run to run (one run seeded at 33.8m/s against an 18m/s truth, another at 2.8-6m/s), and once seeded, the filter wasn't correcting back toward the truth even after many subsequent real measurements. Added a one-shot diagnostic print inside `KalmanBallTracker.SeedFromBuffer` and found the real cause: **every single one of the 8 buffered seed measurements was exactly `(0.000, 0.000, 0.000)`.** This was the same self-referential bootstrapping bug already fixed for Tier 3 (see the third follow-up above — `TriangulateMonocular` needs an existing Z reference, and before any real fix, that reference is a meaningless 0) — but present in a *different*, ungated code path: when `TriangulateStereo` itself self-rejects internally (returns its hardcoded `(0,0,0)` Monocular fallback), `SimulatorEngine`'s "enrich with the Kalman's last Z" logic was *also* using `_tracker.LastState.z`, which is equally meaningless before `HasFix` is true. The `HasFix` guard I'd added earlier only covered the Tier 3 branch, not this Tier 1-self-reject-then-enrich branch. Fixed by applying the same `HasFix` check there: before a real fix exists, a self-rejected stereo attempt now coasts (`TriangulationTier.KalmanOnly`, routed to `Predict()` not `Update()`) instead of feeding a fabricated zero into the seed buffer.

**After this fix**, four consecutive live runs at the 18 m/s test trajectory all converged to **19-20 m/s** — no more run-to-run variance between 2.8 and 33.8, no more decay after seeding, stable through the whole tracked flight. This was very likely the dominant remaining cause of "the ball changes direction/speed unpredictably" — the earlier fixes (dt, least-squares seeding, sub-pixel centroid, spin cap) were all real and necessary, but this bootstrapping bug was corrupting the seed's actual input data regardless of how good the fitting math on top of it was. All 149 tests pass throughout.

This was very likely the dominant remaining cause of "the ball changes direction/speed unpredictably" — the earlier fixes (dt, least-squares seeding, sub-pixel centroid, spin cap) were all real and necessary, but this bootstrapping bug was corrupting the seed's actual input data regardless of how good the fitting math on top of it was. All 149 tests pass throughout.

Position/velocity was now solid, but Nikolas reported the ball still "doing squiggly lines but going straight" in Unity — net displacement roughly correct, path visibly jittery along the way. Confirmed via log: even with the 700rpm plausibility cap holding (see third follow-up), the recovered spin **axis** kept flipping direction almost every reading (`(-0.87,0.46,0.14) → (-0.06,1.00,-0.01) → (-0.97,0.19,0.15) → (0.56,-0.80,0.21) → ...`), and `BallController.ApplyHit` overwrites the ball's Magnus-force spin vector on *every* packet received — far more packets per second than the throttled `[Ball]` log shows. A rapidly, randomly rotating axis reads as exactly this: a jittery/squiggly path whose random perturbations average out to roughly straight net motion, rather than a single clean curve. This is the same underlying issue as the orbiting bug two follow-ups back, just less severe post-cap — magnitude limits can't fix an axis that has no real signal in it, because the mock's ball has no real rotating texture for either spin estimator to measure.

Concluded that chasing tighter thresholds on Spin3D's output was a dead end for mock testing specifically, and disabled spin estimation entirely when `SimulatorEngine` is constructed with a `MockCameraManager` (`_skipSpinEstimation`, checked in `ProcessLoop` before calling `UpdateSpinEstimate`/`UpdateSpin3D`) — `SpinRpm`/`SpinAxis*` now report a clean `0` for the whole mock-tested flight, verified live (no `[Spin3D]` lines at all, `spin=0rpm axis=(0.00,0.00,0.00)` on every sample). Real spin validation still needs a real textured ball on real hardware — this flag only affects the mock path; `CameraManager` (real Spinnaker cameras) is unaffected and will still run both spin estimators normally. All 149 tests pass.

content.thinking:
I found the issue—`maxArea` starts within the valid range but keeps growing over successive frames: 13730, 15770, then climbing through 9544 up to 10528 and beyond. Once it exceeds the 8000 pixel threshold, the contour gets rejected as too large, which is why the ball detection fails.

The steady growth pattern (increasing by roughly 100-200 pixels per frame) is the telltale sign of a moving object leaving a trail in the exponentially-averaged background model. Since the background updates slowly at 95% retention, when the ball moves through a region, that old position lingers in the foreground for about 20 frames before the background fully absorbs it—creating an elongated, comet-tail-like blob that encompasses both the ball's current position and a ghostly trail of where it's been.

With azimuth=0, the ball's motion was mostly radial (shrinking in place as it moved away in Z), so the trail stayed compact. But with non-zero azimuth, the ball sweeps across the screen horizontally as well, creating a longer, wider merged contour that eventually exceeds the MaxContourArea threshold and gets rejected. The core issue is that this simple exponential-moving-average background model fundamentally struggles with laterally-moving objects because the background can't adapt fast enough, and fixing it properly would require either accelerating the decay rate, switching to frame differencing, or implementing motion compensation — all of which represent significant architectural changes.

Since the immediate goal is just to get a test shot moving left without the curved trail artifact, the pragmatic approach is to simply increase how aggressively the background updates each frame, rather than redesigning the entire detection pipeline. I'm looking at the current weighted blend that keeps the background at 95% of its previous state and only incorporates 5% of the new frame — bumping that ratio up would let the background catch up to the ball's trail faster and keep the detected blob tighter.

But I'm realizing this isn't just a mock-specific quirk. A real camera tracking a real ball at high speed would hit the exact same ghosting problem, since any fast-moving foreground object against a rolling-average background naturally creates that trailing effect. So this feels like a genuine issue with the current decay rate that would affect real hardware detection quality too, not just a testing convenience.

Given that real soccer balls move at 10-30 m/s and the camera runs at ~200fps, I'd face similar trail-growth risks if the decay rate isn't tuned aggressively enough. This is worth fixing properly, though the exact optimal rate would need real-world validation eventually. Let me increase the background update rate from 0.05 to something more aggressive like 0.3-0.5, which would make the background catch up much faster each frame and reduce the persistent trail effect. if needed based on what I observe when testing live.

This is a background-subtraction "ghost trail" problem: the rolling background (`AddWeighted(background, 0.95, raw, 0.05, ...)`) only updates 5% toward the current frame each cycle, so it takes ~20 frames to "forget" where the ball used to be. For a ball moving mostly in depth (azimuth=0), that trail stays small and localized. For a ball also sweeping sideways across the sensor, the trail elongates across many distinct pixel positions, merging into one ever-growing contour until it blows past the max area and gets rejected.

Let me try a faster background decay rate — a real fix, not mock-specific, since any real moving ball would hit the same trail-growth issue.

## 2026-07-22 fifth follow-up — a genuinely off-center shot exposed two more real bugs (per-camera background, ghost-trail contour growth)

With straight (azimuth=0) shots solid, Nikolas asked for a shot aimed left-of-center — the first time this session a shot had real, sustained lateral motion instead of mostly-depth motion. Nothing about position/spin worked at all: zero `[Ball]` output regardless of azimuth magnitude (-15°, -8°). This surfaced two more real bugs that a straight-down-the-middle shot happens not to trigger.

1. **`BallDetector` used a single shared background Mat for both cameras.** With `SimulatorEngine` running one `BallDetector` instance for the whole stereo pair, camera 0 and camera 1's frames were diffed against a background that was really an alternating blend of both distinct viewpoints. For a dead-centered shot (both cameras seeing a similar-looking, similarly-positioned view) this blend happened to be harmless by coincidence. With real lateral motion the two views diverge enough that the shared/blended background produces spurious near-identical "detections" in both cameras — confirmed by instrumenting `Triangulator.TriangulateStereo`: a "detected" disparity of ~3px implied a nonsensical depth of 254 meters, nowhere near the ball's real ~3m starting distance. Fixed: `BallDetector` now keeps a `Dictionary<int, Mat>` of backgrounds keyed by `CameraIndex`, so each camera's frames are only ever diffed against its own history. [BallDetector.cs](../Vision/BallDetector.cs)
2. **The rolling background's decay rate (0.95 old / 0.05 new per frame) left a growing "ghost trail."** After fixing bug #1, detection worked briefly then died permanently a few frames later. Instrumented contour area directly and watched it climb steadily frame over frame — 5512 → 7868 → 13730 → ... → 10562px² — until it exceeded soccer's 8000px² ceiling and got rejected for good. The exponential-average background takes ~20 frames to "forget" a pixel the ball recently occupied; for depth-only motion that stale trail stays small and localized (why straight shots worked fine), but a ball sweeping laterally across the sensor leaves a trail spanning many distinct pixel positions, which morphological Close merges into one ever-growing contour with the ball itself. Fixed by making the decay faster (0.7/0.3) so the background catches up within a few frames regardless of travel direction. This is a real, general detection-quality issue — any real ball crossing the frame rather than flying straight back would hit the same growth — not a mock-only patch.

**After both fixes**, two consecutive live runs of a -8° azimuth shot tracked continuously start to finish: X sweeping steadily from 0 to about -2m (left, as intended), Z advancing normally, speed decaying smoothly from ~16 to ~14 m/s, spin holding at a clean 0 throughout (per the fourth follow-up's fix). content.text:
## Summary

Got it working. Aiming left (any non-zero azimuth, really) surfaced two more real bugs that a straight-down-the-middle shot never triggered:

1. **`BallDetector` shared one background model across both cameras.** Diffing each camera's frames against a blended/alternating background happened to be harmless for a centered shot (both views look similar), but a real lateral shot makes the two views diverge enough to produce spurious "detections" — confirmed one such ghost had a disparity implying the ball was 254 meters away. Fixed: separate background per camera (`Dictionary<int, Mat>` keyed by `CameraIndex`).

2. **The background's decay rate left a growing "ghost trail."** After fixing #1, detection worked briefly then died — the contour area was climbing every frame (5512→7868→...→10562px²) until it exceeded the max and got permanently rejected. A ball moving mostly in depth leaves a small, localized trail; one sweeping sideways leaves a trail spanning many pixels that merges into one ever-growing blob. Fixed with a faster background decay (0.7/0.3 instead of 0.95/0.05) — this is a real detection-quality fix, not mock-specific, since any real ball crossing the frame would hit the same issue.

**Result**: `Program.cs` now sets `azimuthDeg: -8f` (kept shallow — the sensor's usable field of view is only ~±11.6°, steeper angles drift the ball out of frame before it's ever tracked). Two consecutive live runs both tracked continuously start to finish: X sweeping from 0 to about -2m (left), Z advancing normally, speed decaying smoothly ~16→14 m/s, spin staying at a clean 0 throughout.

All 149 tests pass. Give it a run in Unity — it should be a clean, straight shot toward the left side of the net now.

content.text:
Good catch to double-check — and you're right that width (720) > height (540), so horizontal FOV actually *is* the wider of the two axes here, not the narrower one. Let me show the actual numbers:

```
horizontal half-angle = atan((720/2) / fx) = atan(360/1757.7)  ≈ 11.6°
vertical half-angle   = atan((540/2) / fx) = atan(270/1757.7)  ≈  8.7°
```

Azimuth is a purely horizontal deflection (`vx = speed·cos(launch)·sin(azimuth)`, `vy` only depends on launch angle, not azimuth), so it's constrained by the **wider** 11.6° horizontal limit — the vertical limit would actually be tighter, at 8.7°. So 11.6° isn't azimuth getting shortchanged by the narrower axis; it's already the more generous of the two.

The reason 11.6° still feels narrow in absolute terms has nothing to do with width vs. height — it's that `fx = 1757.7px` is *large* relative to either sensor dimension. A longer focal length (larger fx, in pixel terms) always narrows the field of view, regardless of which axis you're measuring — that's the dominant factor, not the aspect ratio. This rig's fx was derived from the real on-site FOV measurement (notes: a ~123.5cm × 98cm floor footprint at ~3m distance), so it's effectively a "zoomed in" telephoto setup rather than a wide-angle one — makes sense for precisely tracking a ball at a fixed tee spot, not for capturing a broad scene. That's why even the wider (horizontal) axis only buys ~11.6° before the ball drifts out of frame.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing there are two `[Shot]` events within a 12-second window — the first one appears to be spurious, happening almost immediately at the start with zero velocity, which likely corresponds to the tracker's initialization phase before it had gathered enough samples to properly seed the tracking data.

The issue is that my caching logic doesn't gate on whether the tracker has a valid fix yet; it just checks if detections are real (not Kalman-only), so during those early seeding cycles when velocity is still zero, those detections get cached as shot data. If the coast counter briefly exceeded its timeout early on — perhaps due to a detection gap right at the start — it would prematurely send that zero-velocity garbage as a final shot, reset, and then the real tracking would kick in and produce the correct second shot at the end. This is an edge case bug introduced by my design where an early coast-timeout during the seeding window could trigger a false shot event.

The fix is to add a check for `_tracker.HasFix` to the caching condition, so I only cache and send shot data once the Kalman filter has actually converged with a real velocity estimate, not just whenever real detections arrive.

## 2026-07-22 fifth follow-up — a genuinely off-center shot exposed two more real bugs (per-camera background, ghost-trail contour growth)

With straight (azimuth=0) shots solid, Nikolas asked for a shot aimed left-of-center — the first time this session a shot had real, sustained lateral motion instead of mostly-depth motion. Nothing about position/spin worked at all: zero `[Ball]` output regardless of azimuth magnitude (-15°, -8°). This surfaced two more real bugs that a straight-down-the-middle shot happens not to trigger.

1. **`BallDetector` used a single shared background Mat for both cameras.** With `SimulatorEngine` running one `BallDetector` instance for the whole stereo pair, camera 0 and camera 1's frames were diffed against a background that was really an alternating blend of both distinct viewpoints. For a dead-centered shot (both cameras seeing a similar-looking, similarly-positioned view) this blend happened to be harmless by coincidence. With real lateral motion the two views diverge enough that the shared/blended background produces spurious near-identical "detections" in both cameras — confirmed by instrumenting `Triangulator.TriangulateStereo`: a "detected" disparity of ~3px implied a nonsensical depth of 254 meters, nowhere near the ball's real ~3m starting distance. Fixed: `BallDetector` now keeps a `Dictionary<int, Mat>` of backgrounds keyed by `CameraIndex`, so each camera's frames are only ever diffed against its own history. [BallDetector.cs](../Vision/BallDetector.cs)
2. **The rolling background's decay rate (0.95 old / 0.05 new per frame) left a growing "ghost trail."** After fixing bug #1, detection worked briefly then died permanently a few frames later. Instrumented contour area directly and watched it climb steadily frame over frame — 5512 → 7868 → 13730 → ... → 10562px² — until it exceeded soccer's 8000px² ceiling and got rejected for good. The exponential-average background takes ~20 frames to "forget" a pixel the ball recently occupied; for depth-only motion that stale trail stays small and localized (why straight shots worked fine), but a ball sweeping laterally across the sensor leaves a trail spanning many distinct pixel positions, which morphological Close merges into one ever-growing contour with the ball itself. Fixed by making the decay faster (0.7/0.3) so the background catches up within a few frames regardless of travel direction. This is a real, general detection-quality issue — any real ball crossing the frame rather than flying straight back would hit the same growth — not a mock-only patch.

**After both fixes**, two consecutive live runs of a -8° azimuth shot tracked continuously start to finish: X sweeping steadily from 0 to about -2m (left, as intended), Z advancing normally, speed decaying smoothly from ~16 to ~14 m/s, spin holding at a clean 0 throughout (per the fourth follow-up's fix). All 149 tests pass.

All 149 tests pass.

Also (separately): re-tested the "azimuth off-sensor limit" claimed earlier in this follow-up. It was wrong — made before the two bugs above were found, so it was actually those bugs failing, not a real FOV exit. Retested empirically with them fixed: -15° now tracks cleanly (7 samples), -18° barely works (3 samples, right at the edge), -20°/-25° genuinely fail (off-sensor). Corrected `Program.cs`'s comment and settled on `azimuthDeg: -15f` as a shot with good margin. Also verified (and explained) why `azimuthDeg: 45f` fails: `azimuth` and `launchAngle` are independent parameters in this trajectory model, not components of one combined aim direction — 45° azimuth means 45° of *pure horizontal* deflection (far more extreme than the ~15-18° real limit), not a corner-seeking diagonal shot. The geometric intuition that a rectangular FOV's corner is farther from center than either edge alone is correct, but doesn't apply here since the two angles don't compose that way in this API, and the existing 8° launch angle already sits close to this rig's tighter vertical FOV limit (~8.7°), leaving little vertical headroom regardless.

## 2026-07-22 sixth follow-up — one consolidated shot result per ball, not a continuous stream

Nikolas asked why the middleware was sending 140+ individual `BallData` packets per shot (the throttled `[Ball]` console log only shows every 20th send) rather than one final result, as `notes/11-unity-integration.md`'s original design explicitly called for ("Emit one message to Unity... Unity doesn't need raw frames — it needs the shot result") and as his own earlier `SimulatedHitSender` mock already did. Continuous per-cycle sending was never a deliberate design choice — it's just what `SimulatorEngine.ProcessLoop` had always done, and this session's fixes were all about making that stream *accurate* without anyone stepping back to check whether streaming was the right model at all.

Changed `SimulatorEngine` to cache the latest real (non-`KalmanOnly`) measurement into `_pendingShotData` every cycle instead of sending it immediately, and only actually call `_udp.Send(...)` once — in the Tier 4 coast-timeout branch, exactly when `_coastFrames` exceeds the limit and the ball is judged genuinely gone (`SendPendingShotAndReset`). That single send uses the Kalman filter's fully-converged state as of the last real detection — i.e. its fused best estimate incorporating every measurement across the whole visible flight, which is exactly "one modeled, accurate trajectory taking multiple frames into account," not a separate aggregation step needed. After sending, resets the tracker (`_tracker.Configure`), coast counter, and spin state so the next shot starts clean. Renamed the throttled per-cycle console log from `[Ball]` to `[Tracking]` (diagnostic-only now, no longer indicates a send) and added a distinct `[Shot] Sent final result: ...` line for the actual send event.

Caught one bug in this myself before shipping it: caching on `pt3d.Tier != KalmanOnly` alone wasn't sufficient — the Kalman tracker reports a placeholder zero velocity while still gathering its 8-sample seed buffer (see `KalmanBallTracker.Update`), and those early cycles ARE tagged with a "real" tier (e.g. `FullStereo`) even though `HasFix` is still false. A brief early coast blip during that gathering window sent a spurious `speed=0.0m/s` "shot" before real tracking had even begun. Fixed by additionally gating the cache on `_tracker.HasFix`.

**Verified live**: two consecutive runs each produced exactly one `[Shot]` line, sent at the natural end of tracking. One converged close to the true 18 m/s trajectory (15.3 m/s final); the other undershot (4.2 m/s, following a sharp drop right at a FullStereo→Monocular tier transition) — this is the same underlying Kalman/tracking-quality variance this whole session has been chasing, now visible as a single number instead of buried in a 140-packet stream, not a new bug from this change. All 149 tests pass (no existing test exercised `SimulatorEngine`'s send behavior directly, so nothing needed updating).

content.thinking:
I need to clarify exactly what the final packet contains—whether it's just the raw position from the last frame or if it actually incorporates data from all the frames captured during the shot. Let me trace through the Kalman filter implementation to answer this precisely, starting with how those initial measurements get buffered and processed through the least-squares line fitting.

The key insight is that after those first 8 measurements establish the initial estimate, every subsequent frame triggers the standard Kalman filter update cycle: predict the next state, then correct it with the new measurement. This recursive process is what makes a Kalman filter powerful—each update mathematically fuses the new measurement with the previous state estimate, which already encodes all the information from every earlier measurement weighted by their uncertainty. So the state at any given moment represents a cumulative, weighted fusion of all measurements seen so far, not just the most recent one. The final packet sent contains this cumulative estimate from the last real measurement, meaning it reflects the integrated information from every frame captured throughout the entire tracked flight. The key insight is that this isn't a simple average of all positions—it's a dynamically filtered estimate that accounts for motion and uncertainty, making it far more accurate than just reporting the raw detected position.

content.text:
Yes, exactly — it's not just the last frame's raw position. Every real measurement across the whole tracked flight contributes to the final number, in two stages:

1. **The first 8 measurements** get fit with least-squares (position vs. time, per axis) to get a solid starting velocity/position estimate — already a fusion of 8 samples, not a single one.

2. **Every measurement after that** goes through the Kalman filter's recursive update: predict forward using the current state, then blend that prediction with the new measurement, weighted by how much the filter trusts each (`ProcessNoise` vs `MeasurementNoise`). The critical part: the "current state" going into that blend already reflects *everything measured before it* — that's the whole mechanism of a Kalman filter. So by the time the ball leaves trackable range, the state isn't "the last data point," it's a running fusion of every real detection from the first seed measurement through the last one.

Concretely, in your last run: the final `[Shot]` packet used the Kalman state as of the *last* real measurement — but that state's velocity had already been shaped by every stereo/monocular fix before it, not just that final frame. That's also why the two runs gave different final numbers (15.3 vs 4.2 m/s) even though both used "the same last frame" logic — the whole history leading up to that frame differed between runs, and the filter's fused result reflects that whole history, not a snapshot.

One thing this is *not*: a flat average of raw positions. It also models motion (constant velocity + the process noise assumption), so it's closer to "best physical trajectory consistent with everything I measured" than "average of where I saw the ball."

Good scenario to think through carefully, because the honest answer has some real caveats.

**What actually gets sent isn't a curved path — it's one snapshot.** The middleware measures the ball only during its brief visible window near the tee (a fraction of a second, given the ~3m working distance and the FOV limits we found), then sends one final packet: position, velocity vector, and spin (magnitude + axis) at that moment. It does **not** simulate or send a 3D curved trajectory.

**The actual curving happens entirely in Unity's local physics**, not the middleware. `BallController.ApplyMagnus()` runs every physics frame, computing a continuous sideways force from `cross(spin, velocity)`. So the middleware's job is just to *measure the spin correctly* — the curve itself is Unity's game physics extrapolating from that one spin value for the rest of the flight, well beyond where any camera can see it.

So in principle: **yes**, if the middleware correctly measures a real ball's spin axis and magnitude near the tee, and Unity's Magnus model is a reasonable approximation of real curve physics, a shot that would miss going straight but curves back on target *should* work — that's exactly what Magnus-force game physics is designed to reproduce.

But two real caveats specific to where this project actually stands right now:

1. **For mock testing specifically, spin is completely disabled** (the fix from a few messages ago) — the mock ball has no real rotating texture, so mock shots will never show *any* curve right now, by design. You won't be able to demo this scenario with the mock at all.
2. **For real hardware, spin estimation exists but is explicitly unvalidated** — the code's own comments have said this from the start: "reliability against real ball surfaces under real lighting is UNVALIDATED." Whether it captures a real free-kick's spin accurately enough for this scenario to actually work is an open question, not something proven yet.

There's also a subtler point: even with perfectly accurate spin, Unity's `magnusFactor` and decay tuning are hand-picked "feels right" game values, not physically calibrated against real ball flight data — so the *amount* of curve Unity simulates might not precisely match how much a real ball actually curves, even if the spin *direction* is right.

So the architecture supports what you're describing, but proving it actually works needs real hardware with a real ball, not something the current mock setup can demonstrate.

But the real question is whether such a large cap would actually prevent the 25 m/s divergence we saw — that divergence happened within just one throttle interval after the last good monocular sample, meaning the drift built up very quickly at that higher speed.

Here's the core tension: preventing divergence at high speed requires a tight cap (something ≤20 ticks), but avoiding premature truncation of normal tracking at regular speed requires a much looser cap (≥100+ ticks). The problem is that a fixed tick count doesn't cleanly separate these scenarios, because the real issue isn't about the number of ticks themselves — it's about how much actual time or distance has elapsed.

A time-based cap would be more robust: something like "don't trust monocular Z beyond 100-150ms since the last independent confirmation" would naturally compress into fewer ticks during high-speed scenarios (where the ball covers more distance per tick) and expand into more ticks during slower cadences.

But actually, the real issue isn't wall-clock time or even raw distance traveled — it's how much the true ball position has drifted from what a stale Z prediction assumes, which the Kalman filter's own error covariance already tracks. Instead of imposing arbitrary time or tick limits, I could just monitor the filter's `ErrorCovPost` directly: when it grows large (indicating weak or repeated non-independent measurements), that's the natural signal to stop trusting the monocular Z estimate.

The deeper problem is that my current code treats monocular-derived Z values identically to genuine stereo measurements — feeding both through the same update path with the same measurement noise covariance — when really the filter should be told to trust self-referential Z values less by assigning them higher measurement noise.

A cleaner fix would be to pass a different (weaker) measurement noise specifically for monocular-derived measurements when calling the tracker's update method, but that requires extending the Kalman filter's API to accept per-call noise overrides, which is a more substantial structural change.

Given the time constraints and the back-and-forth on cap values, I'll settle on a middle-ground approach: set a cap around 60-80 cycles (large enough to not truncate normal tracking since a full shot spans roughly 140 cycles, but still bounding worst-case divergence) and test both 18 and 25 m/s to see the practical effect.

This could work two ways: either extend the Kalman tracker to support partial 2D measurements with a modified measurement matrix that only measures X and Y, or more simply, skip feeding monocular ticks into the tracker's update entirely and just use them for display by combining the filter's current Z estimate with the fresh X,Y values from the monocular calculation. poses, so the filter's Z-velocity never gets corrupted by circular feedback. The key insight is treating monocular measurements as predict-only operations for the filter's internal state while still computing a fresh reported position each cycle using the current 2D pixels and the filter's predicted Z—this keeps the Kalman filter clean and eliminates the drift problem entirely.

There's a trade-off though: during a long stereo-loss period, the filter's velocity estimate stays frozen and never adjusts to real changes in motion, but for soccer's short tracking windows with relatively stable velocities, that frozen prediction should hold up fine.

This approach is much cleaner conceptually—never let monocular Z data corrupt the filter, treat all monocular ticks as prediction-only for the filter state while still reporting fresh X/Y coordinates with predicted Z. It eliminates the arbitrary tick-count cap entirely and removes the whole tuning dilemma. I'm going to redesign around this instead, starting by removing the consecutive monocular tick counter. The plan is to strip out the `MaxConsecutiveMonocular` constant and its associated branching logic, keeping just the counter for tracking purposes.

125	## 2026-07-22 sixth follow-up — one consolidated shot result per ball, not a continuous stream
126	
127	Nikolas asked why the middleware was sending 140+ individual `BallData` packets per shot (the throttled `[Ball]` console log only shows every 20th send) rather than one final result, as `notes/11-unity-integration.md`'s original design explicitly called for ("Emit one message to Unity... Unity doesn't need raw frames — it needs the shot result") and as his own earlier `SimulatedHitSender` mock already did. Continuous per-cycle sending was never a deliberate design choice — it's just what `SimulatorEngine.ProcessLoop` had always done, and this session's fixes were all about making that stream *accurate* without anyone stepping back to check whether streaming was the right model at all.
128	
129	Changed `SimulatorEngine` to cache the latest real (non-`KalmanOnly`) measurement into `_pendingShotData` every cycle instead of sending it immediately, and only actually call `_udp.Send(...)` once — in the Tier 4 coast-timeout branch, exactly when `_coastFrames` exceeds the limit and the ball is judged genuinely gone (`SendPendingShotAndReset`). That single send uses the Kalman filter's fully-converged state as of the last real detection — i.e. its fused best estimate incorporating every measurement across the whole visible flight, which is exactly "one modeled, accurate trajectory taking multiple frames into account," not a separate aggregation step needed. After sending, resets the tracker (`_tracker.Configure`), coast counter, and spin state so the next shot starts clean. Renamed the throttled per-cycle console log from `[Ball]` to `[Tracking]` (diagnostic-only now, no longer indicates a send) and added a distinct `[Shot] Sent final result: ...` line for the actual send event.
130	
131	Caught one bug in this myself before shipping it: caching on `pt3d.Tier != KalmanOnly` alone wasn't sufficient — the Kalman tracker reports a placeholder zero velocity while still gathering its 8-sample seed buffer (see `KalmanBallTracker.Update`), and those early cycles ARE tagged with a "real" tier (e.g. `FullStereo`) even though `HasFix` is still false. A brief early coast blip during that gathering window sent a spurious `speed=0.0m/s` "shot" before real tracking had even begun. Fixed by additionally gating the cache on `_tracker.HasFix`.
132	
133	**Verified live**: two consecutive runs each produced exactly one `[Shot]` line, sent at the natural end of tracking. One converged close to the true 18 m/s trajectory (15.3 m/s final); the other undershot (4.2 m/s, following a sharp drop right at a FullStereo→Monocular tier transition) — this is the same underlying Kalman/tracking-quality variance this whole session has been chasing, now visible as a single number instead of buried in a 140-packet stream, not a new bug from this change. All 149 tests pass (no existing test exercised `SimulatorEngine`'s send behavior directly, so nothing needed updating).

Nikolas asked why the middleware was sending 140+ individual `BallData` packets per shot (the throttled `[Ball]` console log only shows every 20th send) rather than one final result, as `notes/11-unity-integration.md`'s original design explicitly called for ("Emit one message to Unity... The sixth follow-up's single-shot design surfaced a real bug in `Triangulator.TriangulateMonocular`: when only one camera detects the ball, its X/Y/Z all derive from a single pixel position plus the Kalman tracker's own last-known Z — not an independent measurement. Feeding that straight into `_tracker.Update()` is circular: the filter "confirms" a value it produced itself, so any small Z-velocity error compounds unboundedly the longer a monocular streak runs. Found live at 25 m/s (faster shots spend longer per real-time interval in this state): the final result diverged to a nonsensical `pos=(10.61,6.61,55.41)`.

First attempt capped how many *consecutive* monocular fixes could feed `Update()` before falling back to coasting (`MaxConsecutiveMonocular`, tried 5 then 15) — both values appeared to cap out almost immediately (frozen final result around Z=9.35m every time, barely past the first couple of real stereo ticks), which looked like the cap was still far too low. That diagnosis was itself wrong, chased down a red herring: those particular test runs were executing a *stale* binary. `dotnet run --no-build` resolves to `bin/Release/net10.0-windows/`, while `dotnet build` for this project (with an implicit x64 platform) writes to `bin/x64/Release/net10.0-windows/` — the two silently diverge, and `--no-build` doesn't fail loud when the binary it finds is old. Running the actual freshly-built exe directly (`./bin/x64/Release/net10.0-windows/SportSimulator.exe`) tells the real story: a queue-backlog check confirmed the process loop keeps up fine with the mock's 200fps generation rate (backlog stayed at 0-2 frames), so throughput was never the issue either.

The real fix needed no threshold at all: route Monocular-tier results through `_tracker.Predict()` instead of `_tracker.Update()` — exactly like a genuine coast tick — so a non-independent measurement can never feed back into the filter's own belief. `MaxConsecutiveMonocular`/`_consecutiveMonocularTicks` were removed entirely as dead weight once this landed. **Verified live** (correct binary): an 18 m/s shot now tracks cleanly through 2 `FullStereo` ticks then dozens of stable `Monocular` ticks (speed locked at 16.7 m/s, no drift) all the way to `[Shot] Sent final result: pos=(3.74,2.65,16.64) speed=16.7m/s`, instead of freezing at ~9.35m. Re-testing the previously-broken 25 m/s case: speed stays locked at 22.9 m/s the whole flight (previously it read a corrupted 4.4 m/s mid-shot) and the trajectory's X/Y/Z ratios stay consistent with the launch/azimuth angles throughout — no divergence. All 149 tests pass.

Also answers a question Nikolas raised about whether launch angle (height) causes frame-exit the same way azimuth does: it doesn't, and the "11.6 degrees" framing from earlier in this doc was already flagged as wrong once the shared-background/ghost-trail bugs were fixed — restated more precisely in `App/Program.cs`'s trajectory comment. The sensor's rejection check (`MockCameraManager.ProjectToCamera`) is a rectangular pixel-bounds test, not a single radial half-angle from center — azimuth (X) and launch angle (Y) push the ball toward different edges of that rectangle, so being close to one axis's limit doesn't consume the other axis's budget. The current 15° azimuth + 14° launch angle shot never exits either camera's frame at all in this session's testing; the ball simply flies far enough in Z to leave *useful stereo range*, which is what ends tracking.

The Tier 3 fix is done, verified, and documented. Summary:

**The real bug and fix**: `TriangulateMonocular`'s X/Y/Z all derive from a single pixel position plus the tracker's own last-known Z — feeding that into `_tracker.Update()` was circular (the filter "confirming" its own prior belief), causing unbounded drift on longer monocular streaks. No cap value fixed this because it's not a threshold problem — it's that `Update()` should never have been called with non-independent data at all. The fix: route `Monocular`-tier results through `Predict()` instead, same as a genuine coast tick. Removed `MaxConsecutiveMonocular`/`_consecutiveMonocularTicks` entirely — no longer needed.

**Why the cap=5/cap=15 tests looked identical and still broken**: those runs were silently executing a stale binary — `dotnet run --no-build` resolves to `bin/Release/`, while this project's build writes to `bin/x64/Release/` (implicit x64 platform), and `--no-build` doesn't warn when it finds an old exe there. Running the real freshly-built binary directly showed the fix working immediately: 18 m/s now tracks through dozens of stable `Monocular` ticks (speed locked at 16.7 m/s) out to `pos=(3.74,2.65,16.64)` instead of freezing at ~9.35m, and the previously-divergent 25 m/s case now holds a locked 22.9 m/s the whole flight instead of corrupting to 4.4 m/s. All 149 tests pass.

**Your height/frame-exit question**: the answer is no, launch angle doesn't cause frame-exit the way azimuth does — that was an over-generalization on my part. `MockCameraManager`'s rejection check is a rectangular pixel-bounds test (`px`/`py` each independently within `[0,SensorW)`/`[0,SensorH)`), not one radial angle from center. Azimuth (X) and launch angle (Y) push toward *different* edges of that rectangle, so being near one axis's limit doesn't eat into the other's budget — your intuition was right. In this session's testing the current 15°/14° shot never exits either camera's frame at all; tracking ends only because Z grows past useful stereo range, which matches your point that velocity/height-so-far is what should matter, not some shared angular budget.

Good, clean and passing. First, correcting the arithmetic, then reporting what I found by actually testing it — because it's more constrained than either of us expected, and points straight at what you were about to propose.

**The math correction:** 200fps means 1 frame every 5ms, not 2 frames per millisecond (that'd be 2000fps) — so 20-30ms is roughly 4-6 frames, not 20-30. That's a real correction, but it doesn't kill your argument — it just means I should go verify the actual number empirically rather than trade estimates.

**What I found by actually instrumenting it:** across the *entire* 2-second simulated flight of the current shot (18 m/s, 17.5°, 15°), the camera pair gets exactly **one** raw detection — a single camera, never both at once, never repeated. Not "fewer than I hoped" — one. I traced why: it's not just the ~0.46m geometric FOV-exit window we calculated — two more things eat into it before any of that even matters:
1. `BallDetector` burns the *first* frame each camera ever sees purely to seed its background-subtraction model — that frame can never produce a detection, by design.
2. As the ball's blob approaches the frame edge, it gets progressively clipped before its center actually crosses the boundary — clipped contour area drops below `MinContourArea` and `BallDetector` rejects it as "not found" *before* the raw pixel math says it's out of bounds.

So the effective window is smaller than the ~5 geometrically-valid frames I calculated, and for this exact trajectory it collapsed to one. I also lowered `KalmanBallTracker`'s `SeedSampleCount` from 8 to 3 (all 149 tests still pass — nothing hardcodes that constant) since 8 was never reachable here regardless, but even 3 doesn't help when only 1 real detection exists at all.

**Your golf-vs-soccer point is the important one, and I think it's right.** Working through my own formula for how fast the ball crosses this narrow vertical FOV: for a fixed launch angle, a *faster* ball reaches the exit boundary *sooner in real time*, not later — meaning golf, being faster, should have this problem *worse*, not better, if the ball starts dead-center like soccer does here. If Accugolf's existing golf pipeline genuinely works starting from center frame, that's strong evidence the working system either (a) doesn't need anywhere near 8 (or even 3) independent samples to get a usable fix, or (b) isn't starting the ball at the exact position I've placed it in this mock.

I don't want to guess which. Can you finish the thought you were cut off on — what specifically did you have in mind changing about the ball's initial position? Given what I've just measured, that's very likely the actual lever here, and I'd rather test the change you're picturing than invent one you didn't mean.

1	# 04 — Hardware Triggering
2	
3	> **Critical for golf.** A free-running camera can't reliably catch the millisecond of impact. You need an external trigger (IR break-beam, mic, photodiode) wired to a GPIO line that fires exposure.
4	
5	## Trigger types
6	
7	| `TriggerSource` value | Meaning |
8	|---|---|
9	| `Software` | Fired by API call (`TriggerSoftware.Execute()`) — useful for testing |
10	| `Line0`, `Line1`, `Line2`, `Line3` | One of the camera's GPIO pins |
11	| `Counter0End`, etc. | Internal counter (advanced) |
12	
13	## Trigger configuration order matters
14	
15	You **must** turn `TriggerMode` **off** before changing source/selector/activation. Then turn it back on. The Spinnaker `Trigger.cpp` example explicitly enforces this order.
16	
17	```cpp
18	// 1. Disable
19	CEnumerationPtr mode = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerMode");
20	mode->SetIntValue(mode->GetEntryByName("Off")->GetValue());
21	
22	// 2. Select WHICH event you're triggering (start of a frame)
23	CEnumerationPtr sel = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerSelector");
24	sel->SetIntValue(sel->GetEntryByName("FrameStart")->GetValue());
25	
26	// 3. Source — hardware Line 0
27	CEnumerationPtr src = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerSource");
28	src->SetIntValue(src->GetEntryByName("Line0")->GetValue());
29	
30	// 4. Edge — rising
31	CEnumerationPtr act = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerActivation");
32	act->SetIntValue(act->GetEntryByName("RisingEdge")->GetValue());
33	
34	// 5. Re-enable
35	mode->SetIntValue(mode->GetEntryByName("On")->GetValue());
36	
37	// Now BeginAcquisition() — frames are gated by Line0 pulses
38	cam->BeginAcquisition();
39	```
40	
41	QuickSpin equivalent (cleaner):
42	```cpp
43	cam->TriggerMode.SetValue(TriggerModeEnums::TriggerMode_Off);
44	cam->TriggerSelector.SetValue(TriggerSelectorEnums::TriggerSelector_FrameStart);
45	cam->TriggerSource.SetValue(TriggerSourceEnums::TriggerSource_Line0);
46	cam->TriggerActivation.SetValue(TriggerActivationEnums::TriggerActivation_RisingEdge);
47	cam->TriggerMode.SetValue(TriggerModeEnums::TriggerMode_On);
48	```
49	
50	## Software trigger fallback (testing)
51	
52	For dev/test without the trigger wiring:
53	
54	```cpp
55	// during config:
56	src->SetIntValue(src->GetEntryByName("Software")->GetValue());
57	
58	// during acquisition loop:
59	CCommandPtr fire = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerSoftware");
60	fire->Execute();
61	ImagePtr img = cam->GetNextImage(1000);
62	```
63	
64	## GPIO physical lines (FLIR cameras)
65	
66	Typical Blackfly S layout:
67	
68	| Line | Wire color | Default function |
69	|---|---|---|
70	| Line 0 | Black | Opto-isolated input (trigger in) |
71	| Line 1 | White | Opto-isolated output (flash/strobe out) |
72	| Line 2 | Red | Bidirectional GPIO |
73	| Line 3 | Yellow | Bidirectional GPIO |
74	
75	Always check the **camera-specific Technical Reference Manual** for pinout — varies by model. The Spinnaker docs only describe the API; pin numbers/colors come from the hardware datasheet.
76	
77	## Strobe output (firing a flash)
78	
79	Mirror image of trigger input. Configure a line as output, point an event at it:
80	
81	```cpp
82	cam->LineSelector.SetValue(LineSelectorEnums::LineSelector_Line1);
83	cam->LineMode.SetValue(LineModeEnums::LineMode_Output);
84	cam->LineSource.SetValue(LineSourceEnums::LineSource_ExposureActive);  // strobe while exposing
85	```
86	
87	Useful if you're using a short-burst LED flash to freeze ball motion further without bumping ISO/gain.
88	
89	## Golf-specific design notes
90	
91	1. **Choose your trigger source.** IR break-beam at the tee is the classic launch-monitor approach. A microphone with peak detection also works (cracks faster than break-beam).
92	2. **Trigger jitter matters.** If your CV pipeline measures ball velocity by Δposition / Δtime, any jitter in trigger-to-exposure delay is a velocity error. Use the same trigger to fire **all** cameras in a multi-cam rig (gang the input wire).
93	3. **Burst mode > single-frame.** Configure `TriggerSelector = FrameBurstStart` and `AcquisitionBurstFrameCount = N` so one trigger pulse → N frames at full rate. That's how you get a sequence of the ball mid-flight.
94	4. **Frame drops on trigger overrun.** Per the example comment: *"if the application/user software triggers faster than frame time, the trigger may be dropped/skipped by the camera."* For multiple frames per trigger use multi-frame / burst mode rather than rapid retriggering.
95	
96	## Trigger overlap (max throughput)
97	
98	To allow a new exposure to start while the previous frame is still reading out:
99	
100	```cpp
101	CEnumerationPtr overlap = nodeMap.GetNode("TriggerOverlap");
102	overlap->SetIntValue(overlap->GetEntryByName("ReadOut")->GetValue());
103	```
104	
105	Important for high-rate burst capture.
106	
107	## Cleanup
108	
109	When done, set `TriggerMode` back to `Off` before `DeInit()` — otherwise the next process to open the camera inherits a triggered camera that won't free-run.
110

content.thinking: The user is asking what an IR break-beam sensor is, so I should explain the concept directly—it's a straightforward factual question about hardware rather than something that needs additional research or tool calls. I'll cover what it is, how it works, and why it would be useful for detecting impact at a golf tee.

content.text:
An IR break-beam sensor is a simple two-part detector: an infrared LED emitter on one side, and a photodiode/phototransistor receiver on the other, facing each other so the receiver normally sees a steady beam of infrared light. When something passes between them — physically blocking the beam — the receiver's signal drops out for that instant, and that dropout is used as a trigger pulse. It's the same principle as a driveway/garage-door safety sensor, or the beam you break walking through a convenience-store door.

For a launch monitor, you'd mount the emitter and receiver on either side of the ball's rest position (or just in front of it, along the path the club/ball will cross), aimed so the ball or clubhead breaks the beam right at (or just before) impact. That break event fires an electrical pulse, which gets wired into the camera's GPIO trigger input (`Line0` per the notes) — so the camera's exposure timestamp is tied directly to that physical moment, with sub-millisecond precision, rather than being inferred from whichever video frame happened to catch the ball first.

Compared to the microphone alternative also mentioned in the notes (detecting the "crack" sound of impact via peak detection): break-beam fires slightly earlier and more consistently (a sound has to travel and be filtered/thresholded; light-blocking is closer to instantaneous), but it requires the ball or club to physically cross a specific line, so mounting position matters — it needs to be placed somewhere the ball or club face reliably passes through on every shot.

Based on standard SpinView layout (same GenICam categories the project's own notes already reference for `TriggerSource`/`TriggerMode`, just a different category):

1. Open SpinView and connect to the camera (double-click it in the camera list, or select it and click the connect/play icon) — this opens the live image view plus a **Camera Control** panel, usually docked on the right.
2. In that Camera Control panel, the settings are grouped into collapsible categories — the same place you'd have found `TriggerMode`/`TriggerSource` under **Acquisition Control**. Look instead for a category called **Digital IO Control** (sometimes written **Digital I/O Control**).
3. Inside that category, there are two related fields:

4. Since `Line Status` only shows one line at a time, cycle the `Line Selector` through all four lines and watch each one while doing your test action. If your version of SpinView also exposes **Line Status All**, that's more convenient — it shows all four lines at once as a single bitmask, so you don't have to keep switching the selector.

If the categories aren't laid out exactly like that in your SpinView version, most versions have a small search/filter box above the property tree — typing "line" there should surface all the Line-prefixed fields regardless of which category they're nested under.

content.text:
**Root cause and fix, in full:**

The ball went backward because `Triangulator`'s reported Z was measured along the camera's own tilted optical axis, which points *toward the tee* (backward), not toward the net — so Z decreased as the ball actually flew forward, and that negative Z-velocity got sent straight to Unity. This is exactly the deferred "world-frame rotation" issue (#2) we flagged earlier, surfacing now because the mock finally models the real tilt correctly.

Implemented the fix in `Triangulator.ToWorldFrame`: X is re-centered onto the stereo pair's baseline midpoint (was relative to camera0's own axis), and Y/Z are rotated out of the camera's tilted local axis into true world coordinates (Y up, Z toward the net). `TriangulateMonocular` and `KalmanBallTracker`'s rest position got simplified accordingly — the tee is genuinely `(0,0,0)` in world coordinates now, and the old `-pt3d.Y` flip in `SimulatorEngine` is gone since Triangulator returns properly-signed Y-up directly.

Building it caught a real bug along the way: hand-verifying live output isn't reliable (different noise draws each run), so I wrote a controlled round-trip test — project a known world point through the same math the mock uses, feed it through `TriangulateStereo`, check you get the original point back. It caught a genuine sign error immediately (Y ended up in the wrong quadrant) that hand-checking noisy output never would have — `Triangulator`'s raw Y is Y-down (standard pinhole convention), and my rotation formula needed a Y-up input; I'd wired them together without accounting for that. Fixed, and those three round-trip tests are now permanent regression coverage against this exact class of bug.

**Final live result, 5/5 runs:** `pos=(0.11, 0.12, 0.41)`, speed=17.1 m/s — Z positive (toward net), Y positive (rising, matches 17.5° launch), X positive (rightward, matches 15° azimuth). All 152 tests pass, stable across repeated runs. This should now go the right way in Unity — worth testing there to confirm.

content: what is does the azimuth degree mean?

message.content: what is does the azimuth degree mean?

content.thinking: The user is asking what azimuth means in the context of the SetTrajectory method, so I should explain that it represents the horizontal direction or compass bearing of the projectile's launch, distinct from the launch angle which controls elevation. I can tie this to how the code decomposes the velocity vector using both angles to calculate the actual x, y, and z components of motion.

content.text:
"Azimuth" here is the *horizontal* aim direction — which way left or right the shot is aimed, independent of how high it's launched. It's a term borrowed from navigation/astronomy (compass bearing relative to a reference direction), and in this codebase it's the angle relative to straight down the middle of the net.

Concretely, from `MockCameraManager.GenerateFrames`, the shot's velocity gets split into three components:
```
vz = speed·cos(launchAngle)·cos(azimuth)   // depth — how fast it flies downrange
vx = speed·cos(launchAngle)·sin(azimuth)   // lateral — how fast it drifts left/right
vy = speed·sin(launchAngle)                 // vertical — how fast it rises
```
So `azimuthDeg` and `launchAngleDeg` are two *independent* dials, not one combined "aim direction": azimuth controls left-right, launch angle controls up-down. `azimuthDeg: 0` is dead straight down the middle; increasing the magnitude sweeps the shot further to one side, purely horizontally, regardless of how the launch angle is set.

The sign convention in this project (confirmed against Unity's own `GoalkeeperAI` logic): **positive azimuth = rightward drift, negative = leftward** — matches positive world X → positive Unity X → `GoalkeeperAI` reading positive ball X as the right side of the net. So the current config (`azimuthDeg: 15f`) is a shot aimed 15° to the right of center, combined separately with a 25° launch angle for height.

content.text:
Good catch — that was a real gap. Here's what changed:

**The fix:** in `KalmanBallTracker.Update()`, a displacement is no longer enough by itself to trigger a shot. The ball must first be confirmed resting for `MinRestSamplesForConfidence` (5) consecutive agreeing samples — roughly 25ms at 200fps. If it moves before reaching that, the system treats it as still being placed: it resets the candidate rest position to the new spot and keeps waiting, rather than firing a false shot. Since real players pause far longer than 25ms before actually striking the ball, this shouldn't get in the way of any genuine shot.

I also removed the confidence-scaling code I'd added in the previous step — with this gate in place, every triggered shot always has at least the minimum sample count, so that scaling always evaluated to 1.0 and was dead weight.

**Test fallout:** 4 existing tests fed continuous motion starting from frame 0 (simulating an already-in-flight object) — under the new gate, that pattern correctly never resolves to a fix, since it never looks like "resting, then displaced." Fixed by prepending a proper resting phase to each, matching how any real shot actually starts. A fifth test (`StationaryBall_VelocityConvergesToZero`) still passed but for a more direct reason now — updated its comment to reflect that.

All 152 tests pass, stable across repeated runs, and live mock testing still produces consistent, correctly-signed shots. This is still a heuristic, not a certainty, though — it narrows the false-positive window from "any single displaced sample" down to "displaced *after* a confirmed real settling period," but it can still in principle be fooled by someone pausing for the full 25ms mid-placement. That residual ambiguity is exactly what a real hardware trigger would eliminate entirely, which is still the open question from earlier.

I need to think through what `StereoCalibrator.AddFramePair()` actually expects and how stereo calibration works in practice.

The key insight is that stereo calibration fundamentally requires the SAME physical checkerboard visible to BOTH cameras at the same time, since the algorithm needs to match corner points between the left and right images of identical physical locations in space—this is how it computes the relative rotation and translation between the cameras. Using two separate checkerboards would break this correspondence entirely. So you're working with one board that you move to different positions and angles between captures, ensuring both cameras see it fully in each frame for a well-conditioned calibration. So the board needs to stay within that narrow visible cone the cameras can actually see—basically positioned around the tee area where the ball address is, but held at various heights and slight offsets (left/right, closer/farther) to capture the distortion effects across the full image plane. Since the cameras are mounted quite high, I'm thinking about the practical logistics of how someone would actually hold and move the board during calibration. Across each capture, I need to vary the distance, tilt angle, and position within the frame while ensuring all 9×6 inner corners stay fully visible and unclipped—otherwise the corner detection will fail. Given how narrow this rig's field of view actually is, the practical capture zone is really just confined near the ground at the tee, which is quite different from a typical wide-FOV calibration setup where you'd move the board freely around a room, so I should set that expectation clearly to avoid wasted attempts.

content.text:
**One checkerboard, not two** — stereo calibration needs both cameras looking at the *same physical board* at the same moment, so it can match corresponding corner points between the left and right images and figure out their relative positions. Two different boards wouldn't give it anything to match up.

**Where to place it — and this matters more than usual given this specific rig:** this camera pair has a genuinely narrow field of view (confirmed earlier this session: ~11.6° horizontal half-angle, ~8.7° vertical, aimed steeply down at the tee/address spot). The board has to be *within that narrow cone* for both cameras to see it at all — which in practice means holding it near the ground, right around where the ball normally sits, not out at eye level or off to the side. If you hold it somewhere the cameras aren't actually aimed, both `FindChessboardCorners` calls will just fail and the tool will tell you to reposition.

Within that same tee-area zone, vary it across your ~15-20 captures:
- **Distance** — a bit closer to the cameras, a bit farther, not the same spot every time
- **Position in frame** — not dead-center every capture; corners of the frame too
- **Tilt** — angle the board somewhat rather than holding it perfectly flat/perpendicular each time

That variation is what lets calibration properly separate lens distortion from the cameras' relative pose — a bunch of captures at the exact same spot and angle would actually calibrate worse than fewer, more varied ones. Just make sure, for each capture, all 9×6 inner corners are fully in frame for *both* cameras — if the board's edge gets clipped in either view, that specific capture will fail (the tool reports this per-attempt, so you'll know right away and can just reposition and retry).

Both — and the mix matters here more than usual because of what this calibration actually needs to support.

Do a good number of captures **on/near the ground** at different positions (this directly matches the majority of what the system tracks — the ball's rest position and the early part of its flight, right near the ground plane), and a good number held **at varying heights above the ground** (simulating where the ball actually is as it rises during flight — height accuracy is exactly what this session's work has been most concerned with getting right).

content: dotnet run -f net48 -- --calibrate is the command? what does the -- with nothing after it do?

message.content: dotnet run -f net48 -- --calibrate is the command? what does the -- with nothing after it do?

content.thinking:
The user is asking about the `--` syntax in a `dotnet run` command. The double-dash acts as a separator between options meant for `dotnet run` itself (like `-f net48` to specify the target framework) and arguments that should be passed directly to the application being run (like `--calibrate`).

Without the `--`, the CLI tool might try to interpret `--calibrate` as its own flag and error out, but with it, everything after the separator gets passed through to the program's `args` array unchanged. This is a standard POSIX convention used across many CLI tools like npm and cargo. I should also walk through the full command syntax including that optional second argument for the output path, and show a concrete example to make the whole thing clearer.

content.text:
Good question — `--` is a separator, not an argument itself. It marks the boundary between "options meant for the `dotnet` CLI tool" and "arguments meant to be passed through to the actual program being run."

Breaking down `dotnet run -f net48 -- --calibrate`:
- `dotnet run` — build and run the project
- `-f net48` — a flag *for `dotnet run` itself*, picking which target framework to use (needed since this project targets both `net48` and `net10.0-windows`)
- `--` — "everything after this point isn't for `dotnet run` — pass it straight through to my program's `args`"
- `--calibrate` — the actual argument your program receives, which `Program.cs` checks for

Without the `--`, `dotnet run` would try to interpret `--calibrate` as one of *its own* flags (which doesn't exist), and error out rather than forwarding it to your app. This is a common convention across a lot of CLI tools (npm, cargo, etc.) — the bare `--` always means "stop parsing my own options here."

So there are two separate tokens involved, not one: the bare `--` (separator) and `--calibrate` (your program's own argument, which just happens to also start with dashes because that's the convention I used when wiring it up in `Program.cs`).

If you also want to specify a custom output path instead of the default `stereo_calibration.json`, it'd be: `dotnet run -f net48 -- --calibrate my_calibration.json`.

2. When prompted for a username, enter your GitHub username

Given the tool's minimum of 15 pairs and the principle that more is better, I'm thinking 20-25 total captures would give a comfortable margin, with roughly 60-70% at or near ground level (varying across the tee area) and 30-40% at elevated heights (up to a foot or two, matching the realistic flight range this session's analysis has already pinned down). The real goal is ensuring good coverage across the full 3D volume where the system will operate, with variety in all three axes. So I should spread those captures across both axes—varying X position and tilt angle for ground-level shots, and doing the same for elevated positions at different heights—rather than just changing one dimension at a time. A balanced split around 8-10 captures near ground and 8-10 at varying heights would give me 16-20 total, well above the minimum while keeping height calibration equally constrained. content.text:
Roughly an even split — I wouldn't weight it heavily toward one or the other. Something like **half near ground level, half held up at varying heights** works well, and here's why it's not more lopsided than that: calibration accuracy is best where you've actually given it data, and this session's whole focus has been on getting the *height/vertical* dimension right (the world-frame rotation fix) — so under-sampling elevated positions would leave exactly the dimension you care most about the least well-calibrated.

Concretely, for a target of ~20 total captures (comfortably above the 15 minimum):
- **~8-10 near ground level** — varying X position across the tee area and varying tilt (don't just lay it flat every time — angle it differently too)
- **~8-10 elevated** — varying both height (up to that foot-or-two range we discussed earlier, matching where the ball's real trajectory actually goes) *and* position/tilt, not just holding the same spot higher up

The key thing either way: don't vary just one thing at a time (e.g., all ground shots at the same tilt, or all elevated shots at the same height). Cross the variety — different position *and* different height *and* different tilt across the full set — since that's what actually lets calibration separate lens distortion from the cameras' pose, rather than just sampling one slice of the space thoroughly.

content.text:
The image confirms what you found: `Line Selector` is on Line 3, `Line Mode` = Input, and `Line Status All` reads `0xC` (binary `1100` — Line2 and Line3 sitting high, Line0 and Line1 low). That's a static bitmask, not something that moved when you stepped into frame. Combined with your report that none of the four lines changed as you moved into view, this is solid: **there's no hardware sensor wired to this camera's trigger inputs.** The `0xC` you're seeing is just the idle electrical state of unused GPIO pins (pull-up/pull-down resistors, or simply floating inputs reading a fixed level) — not a live signal from anything watching for impact. That IR panel on the unit is almost certainly just an illuminator, not a shot sensor.

Practically: this confirms the camera-inferred rest-position/settling approach already built into the middleware is the right (and only) path here — there's no external trigger to fall back on or supplement it with. Nothing to change in the code; this was a diagnostic dead-end in the good sense — it closes the question.

On the checkerboard — 1 success out of ~50 at closer range tells us size wasn't the only problem. At the golf-tee distance (~3m) the board was too small to detect reliably; moving closer made it detectable in principle but now something else is failing almost every time. The two most likely culprits, and how to tell them apart without any new equipment:

1. **Lens focus/depth-of-field** — these are fixed-focus lenses tuned for the ~3m working distance. Closer than that, the board may be visibly blurred to the point `FindChessboardCorners` can't lock onto corners. Check this directly: have SpinView open (or add a quick preview flag) and just look at the live image with the board close — if it's visibly soft/blurry, that's your answer, and closer distance is not viable at all.
2. **Stereo parallax** — at close range the two cameras' significant baseline separation means the board might be nicely centered in one camera's view but cut off or heavily skewed in the other. This would show as inconsistent success (sometimes one camera fails, not always the same one) rather than uniform blur in both.

Given the fixed-focus constraint, I'd lean toward this being a losing battle at close range — the real fix is a **larger true-size board** (A1 or A2 from that same site) so it's big enough to detect at the actual ~3m working distance without needing to move closer at all. That avoids both the focus and parallax problems simultaneously. Since you're at the rig right now, the fastest way to confirm before ordering/printing anything: check if the SpinView live image looks sharp when you hold the board at ~3m even though corners aren't detecting (if it's sharp, size alone is confirmed as the entire problem, and a bigger board will just work) vs. blurry (in which case working distance itself needs revisiting, not just board size).

Want me to add a `--calibrate --preview` style flag to `CalibrationRunner` that dumps the raw captured frame to a file so you can inspect sharpness without needing SpinView open separately? That'd let you check focus quality directly from the same tool instead of context-switching.

content.text:
Nice — 30 pairs with varied position/angle/height is exactly the mix that gives a good, well-conditioned calibration (much better than the minimum 15, and much better than all-same-distance shots). "Dead zones" where it wouldn't detect are expected and not a red flag by themselves — most likely explanations, roughly in order of likelihood:

- **Edge-of-FOV / stereo non-overlap** — near the outer edges of either camera's view, or spots visible to one camera but not the other (or only partially), corner detection in that camera alone will fail even if the board looks fine to your eye.
- **Off-axis tilt** — a checkerboard turned edge-on to one of the two cameras foreshortens badly enough that `FindChessboardCorners` can't resolve the grid, even though it works fine face-on a few inches away.
- **Local blur/glare** — a spot that happens to catch harsh light or sit right at the focus boundary for one camera.

None of that is a problem as long as your 30 accepted pairs span a good spread of the working volume (which sounds like they do) — you don't need every spot in the volume to succeed, just enough varied good ones.

Next: did the tool finish and print an RMS reprojection error? If so, what number did it show — under ~1.0px is good, higher and it's worth recapturing a few more varied pairs before trusting it.
